Every subwoofer rental on this page arrives with a crew: we bring the subs, place them, tune them, sound check them with your source and come back after the event to take them away, and all of that is included in the rental. We run the cabling and we set the tuning ourselves, so your DJ or engineer walks up to a system that is already working, and delivery and pickup are ours.
1
### Intake
Venue, date, guest count, music and load in rules. We advance power, elevator access and curfew with the venue rather than assuming.
2
### Delivery and placement
We deliver and place the subs where the room wants them, which is rarely where they fit most neatly. Placement changes the low end more than volume does.
3
### Tuning
Crossover, gain and delay set to the room, checked from the dance floor and the back wall, not from behind the rig.
4
### Sound check and pickup
We sound check the system with your DJ or your mixing console, your side runs the show, and after the event we come back to strike and load out. Coiling, counting and returning are all ours.
### Delivery and setup included
Every rental on this page includes delivery and pickup by our crew. The same people who load the truck are the ones who tune the rig at the venue, which is why a typical job is working before anyone on your side arrives.
### Power planned before the date
A typical venue circuit will not carry a full rig on its own. We work out the circuits with the venue in advance and bring distro when the room needs it.
### Insured and certificate ready
Most DFW hotels and convention venues want a certificate of insurance naming them. Tell us the venue at intake and we send it before you are chased for it.
### Spare boxes on the truck
We carry more than the plan calls for. If a room turns out to be bigger, louder or more open than the walkthrough suggested, the extra sub is already there.
### Sound checked with your source
The person who tuned the system sound checks it with your DJ or your mixing engineer before doors, with the gain matched to your console or controller, so the first song plays through a rig that is already dialed in.
### One crew, one contract
Audio, lighting and effects come from the same company on the same load in, so the whole build finishes on one clock.
The boxes
## Why we run BASSBOSS subwoofers and tops
We settled on BASSBOSS for the DFW rental fleet for reasons that show up on a job rather than on a spec sheet. Every box is self-powered, so the amplifier and processing live inside the cabinet: fewer road cases, a faster load in, and every amplifier cooled inside its own cabinet. They hold their level through a full night instead of tightening up after the first hour, and they are voiced for the bass heavy music most of our clients book. If you want the longer version, we wrote one: why we use BASSBOSS speakers and subwoofers for Dallas events .
These are the four boxes we rent most. Picking one is our job. Tell us the room and the music and we will tell you which of these belongs under it.
Top
### BASSBOSS DV12 speakers
Box Single 12 inch powered top · pole mount · singles, pairs or a 2x2 array
The DV12 is the top box that goes above the subs on most of our jobs. It carries vocals and music cleanly at distance and keeps its pattern controlled, so a long room sounds the same at the back as at the front. It scales with the sound unchanged: one for a small room, a pair for most receptions, four in a 2x2 arrangement when a room is wide. Because it is powered, adding a box means adding a box, not rebuilding an amp rack.
Best for Mobile DJs, receptions, corporate general sessions and any room where the tops have to reach the back.
Sub
### BASSBOSS SSP118 subwoofers
Box Single 18 inch powered sub · the standard building block
The SSP118 is the sub we rent most, and it is the one we mean when we say one sub or two subs above. A single 18 inch box that reaches deeper and holds level better than a typical rental sub of the same size, which usually means fewer boxes on the truck for the same result in the room. It is also the easiest sub here to scale: start with one, add a second when the room grows, and you get more impact with the character of the low end intact.
Best for Weddings, private parties, mobile DJ work, corporate events and smaller venues.
Sub
### BASSBOSS VS21 subwoofers
Box Single 21 inch powered sub · deep extension with punch
A single 21 inch driver moves considerably more air than an 18, and the VS21 uses it for two things at once: it goes deeper, and it keeps the transient impact that makes a kick drum feel physical rather than just loud. That combination is why it is our default when the booking is a club night, a bass heavy DJ set or a band with a serious rhythm section. It stays musical when it is being pushed instead of pumping audibly.
Best for EDM, dubstep, drum and bass, rap and hip hop, and live bands on a real stage.
Sub
### BASSBOSS ZV28 subwoofers
Box Dual 18 inch powered sub · the largest box we deploy routinely
The ZV28 is what we bring when the low end has to reach a crowd rather than a room: two 18 inch drivers in one cabinet, reaching low frequencies consistently and staying controlled at a level where a typical sub has already turned into a rumble. It is the headline box on this list, and the deep, clean bottom it produces is the reason a festival or a warehouse show is a different conversation from a wedding. Across a floor that size the impact stays even, so the back of the crowd feels what the front feels.
Best for Festivals, warehouse shows, large outdoor stages and big dance floors.
### The larger BASSBOSS boxes are available too
Beyond the four above we can source the bigger families in the BASSBOSS line, including the double and quad 21 inch subs and the MFLA line array modules, for shows that genuinely need them. That is a production conversation rather than a rental form, so tell us the stage size and the expected crowd and we will scope it properly.
Concerts and festivals
## Concert sound system rental in Dallas
Rig Line array or point source tops · sub block · monitors · engineer
A concert is its own job. It has an input list, a stage plot, a support act, a changeover and someone whose whole job is monitors. When a promoter or a band asks us for a concert sound system in Dallas, what they are really asking for is a rig that holds up at show level for four hours and a crew who has run a changeover before. The BASSBOSS boxes described above are what we build that rig from.
The low end is where most rented concert systems fall down, because they are sized for the room and not for the crowd. A room absorbs very little; five hundred people absorb a great deal. We size the sub count against the crowd and the genre, arrange the boxes so the bass lands on the audience rather than the back of the stage, and keep headroom in hand so the system is loafing during the headliner. On a typical festival stage that headroom is the difference between impact and distortion by the third act.
For loudspeakers above the subs, most shows past a few hundred people move to line array speaker rental , and we quote the two together because splitting them across vendors is how a system ends up untuned. If you are booking a band rather than a festival, the live music and band events page covers backline, monitors and input lists.

Clubs, raves and warehouse shows
## Club and rave sound system rental
Dallas has a real underground scene, and the rooms it happens in were built for something else. Warehouses, empty retail units, patios, art spaces and rooms with a concrete floor and a metal ceiling all share the same acoustics: enormous reflections and bass that runs free. A rig that sounds enormous at the door can be unlistenable in the middle of the floor, and adding volume makes it worse rather than better.
### Warehouse and open shell rooms
Hard walls send everything back at you. We aim the tops down onto the crowd instead of across the room, keep the subs off the corners where they load up, and accept a slightly lower level for a much deeper one. Bass in a warehouse comes from arrangement, not from turning it up.
### Club installs and takeovers
Plenty of DFW venues have a house system that is fine for a bar night and short for a headliner. We can supplement the house rig with subs and tops for the night, then take it back out, so the venue keeps its install and the promoter gets the show they sold.
### Neighbors, curfews and complaints
Low frequencies travel further than anything else and they travel through walls. Where the room has neighbors we arrange the subs to keep the energy on the dance floor and off the property line, and we set a level plan for the night at load in rather than at midnight.
### The DJ booth is part of the rig
A booth with proper monitoring means a DJ mixing on time, instead of off the room's echo. Booth monitors, a clean feed and decks that are already tested are included in the setup. CDJ rental covers the decks themselves.
### Lights, lasers and haze on the same call
Most of these shows want more than sound. Lasers , moving heads and a hazer to make the beams visible all come from the same crew and the same truck.
### Power for an unbuilt room
Warehouses often have power that was designed for lights and forklifts. We work out the available circuits during a walkthrough, bring distro, and plan for a generator when the building needs the help.
### Running a club night or a rave in DFW?
The rave and night club events page covers how we work with promoters, including walkthroughs, load in windows and what we need from the venue. You can also look through the photo gallery to see real DFW events we have run.
Speaker rentals by room
## Speaker and subwoofer rentals for parties, venues and outdoor events
The room decides the rig more than the guest list does. These are the DFW spaces we work in most, and what changes about the low end in each of them.
### Backyards and tentsPrivate parties, graduation, birthdays
Rig 1 to 2 subs · tops on poles · house power checked first
Open air gives the bass nowhere to reflect from, so a backyard needs more low end than a typical indoor room of the same size to feel the same. Tents help slightly. The other backyard variable is power: house circuits are shared with everything else on the property, and a rig on the same breaker as the kitchen is a problem waiting for the first course. Private events covers the rest.
### Hotel ballroomsWeddings, galas, corporate dinners
Rig 2 subs · 2 to 4 tops · hotel load in advanced
A typical DFW hotel ballroom holds low end well, sometimes too well, and a boomy room is usually a placement problem rather than a volume one. Hotels also have the strictest load in rules of any venue we work in, so dock times, elevators and certificates get advanced days ahead. See weddings and corporate events .
### Breweries, barns and event hallsReceptions, launches, community events
Rig 2 subs · 4 tops · coverage split across the space
These rooms are long, hard surfaced and usually have a bar at the opposite end from the dance floor. One rig aimed at everything makes the dance floor painful and the bar inaudible, so we split coverage and keep the subs on the floor rather than trying to serve both ends from one stack.
### Warehouses and raw spacesRaves, art events, pop ups
Rig 4 or more subs · tops aimed down · distro or generator
Everything about a raw space is a reflection problem and a power problem. We walk these rooms before the date whenever we can, because only a walkthrough tells you what the ceiling is made of, and a typical rig that works in a hall will disappoint in a shell.
### Campus venuesUniversity, school and college events
Rig Sized to the space · campus safety and power approvals
Gyms and student unions are reflective, and campuses have their own approvals process on top of the venue's. We handle that paperwork with the department rather than leaving it with a student committee. See college and university events .
### Outdoor stages and lotsFestivals, block parties, city events
Rig 4 or more subs · line array tops · weather plan
Outdoors the sub count goes up, the arrangement gets deliberate, and there is a weather plan for the rig as well as for the event. Sound carries a long way over a parking lot, so we plan the level and the aim around what is on the other side of the fence.
### Bars and patiosResidencies, small live music, DJ nights
Rig 1 sub · 2 tops · compact footprint
A typical bar room wants a rig that gives the dance floor real low end while conversation six feet away at the bar carries on. That is a placement and tuning job more than an equipment one, and it is where a tuned rental beats a bigger untuned one every time.

## Rent subwoofers to go under your own tops
Rig Subs only · crossover and gain matched to your boxes on site
Plenty of the rentals we run on this page are low end only. Where speech matters as much as music, our microphone rentals run through an AI-powered De-Feedback system that suppresses feedback before anyone in the room hears it, which is what lets a handheld work in a bright room. There is a plain explanation of how De-Feedback works on the blog.

## Subwoofer rental questions we get asked
How many subwoofers do I need for my event?
It depends on guest count, music style, and whether the room is enclosed. As a rough guide, one sub covers up to about 100 guests indoors, two subs suit most receptions of 100 to 250, and 250 guests and up usually wants four or more. Bass heavy genres and outdoor events both push that number higher. Tell us the venue and the head count and we will size it properly.
Do you deliver and set up subwoofer rentals in Dallas and Fort Worth?
Yes. Every rental is full-service. We deliver, place and tune the rig, sound check it with your DJ or your mixing console, then come back after your event to strike and load out. Delivery, setup, tuning and pickup are all included rather than added.
What areas do you serve around Dallas-Fort Worth?
We commonly serve Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Irving, Grapevine, Plano, Frisco, Richardson and Denton, within roughly a forty mile radius of ZIP 76053. Outside that, ask about availability and we will tell you honestly whether it works for your date.
What is included in a rental?
Dallas Event Audio is a full-service company, so delivery, setup, a sound check with your audio source and pickup are part of every rental. That is also why the rig arrives tuned and working rather than as a pile of boxes.
Can I rent subwoofers only and use my own tops or the venue PA?
Yes. We regularly put rented BASSBOSS subs under a band's own PA, a DJ's tops or a venue's house system. Send us the make and model of your tops at intake and we will match the crossover and gain to them on site.
Do you rent BASSBOSS speakers as well as subwoofers?
Yes. We rent BASSBOSS DV12 powered tops individually, in pairs or as a 2x2 array, alongside the SSP118, VS21 and ZV28 subs. Tops and subs are usually quoted together so the system is matched.
Which subwoofer suits deep bass and dubstep drops?
For the deepest extension on a large floor, the ZV28. For deep bass with hard transient impact, the VS21. For a powerful single 18 inch building block that scales as the room grows, the SSP118. We will recommend one after hearing the venue and the set.
Are these systems good for EDM, house, drum and bass, rap and hip hop?
Yes. The fleet is chosen for bass heavy music, with deep extension and the transient impact that makes a kick feel physical rather than only loud. These are the same rigs we run for club nights and warehouse shows across DFW.
Do I need to supply power for a subwoofer rental?
Usually the venue's power is enough, but it has to be the right circuits rather than whatever is nearest. We advance power with the venue before the date and bring distro when the room needs it. For warehouses and outdoor sites we will plan for a generator.
How far in advance should I book a subwoofer rental?
Two to four weeks is comfortable for most events, and longer for peak wedding and holiday dates. Short notice is often still possible, so call us rather than assuming it is too late.

## How many speakers does your party or event need?
This is the first question almost everyone asks, and the answer starts with three things: how many people are in the room, what the music is, and whether there are walls. Seventy-five guests in a banquet room and seventy-five guests in an open backyard want different rigs, because a room keeps the sound and a backyard gives it away. Below is how we size a DJ speaker rental in practice. Tell us the venue and the head count and we will tell you which line you are on.
### Up to 75 guestsHouse party, backyard, small hall
Rig 2 powered tops on poles · one 20 amp circuit
A pair of powered 12 inch or 15 inch tops on stands covers a room this size with headroom left over. Height is what matters more than box count here: speakers up on poles put the sound over people's heads instead of into the back of whoever is standing in front of them. The trap at this size is a rig set too loud for a small space, which is why we set the level standing at the far end of the room rather than behind the gear.
### 75 to 200 guestsReception, brewery, banquet room
Rig 2 tops · 1 sub · separate circuit for the sub
This is where most DFW receptions and company parties land, and it is the point where a subwoofer stops being optional. Once a dance floor fills, bodies absorb low end, and a pair of tops on their own start working hard to make up for it. Adding a sub takes that job off the tops, so the vocals stay clear while the floor gets its weight. It is also the point where the low end wants a circuit of its own, and we work that out with the venue before the date instead of at load in.
### 200 to 400 guestsClub night, school dance, large reception
Rig 4 tops · 2 subs · dedicated power drop
At this size a single pair of tops in one corner leaves the far end of the room guessing. Four tops let us cover a long or wide space evenly, so the people by the bar hear the same mix as the people on the floor. Two subs placed together also couple, which gives deeper and more even bass across the dance floor rather than one hot spot in the middle of it. This is the size where we start asking for a dedicated power drop rather than sharing with the caterer.
### 400 guests and upWarehouse, outdoor stage, festival
Rig Line array tops · 4 or more subs · distro and a power plan
Past four hundred people a pole mounted top runs out of reach, and the conversation moves to line array speaker rental with a sub block underneath. Outdoors the sound has open air to fill, so the box count goes up and the arrangement matters as much as the number: speakers can be aimed so the sound lands on the crowd and stays off the neighbors. That comes up more often in Dallas than people expect, and it is worth planning before a noise complaint plans it for you.
### Bass heavy musicEDM, house, drum and bass, rap and hip hop
Rig Add a sub per pair of tops · or step up a box size
Guest count is only half the sizing question. A jazz trio and a house set with the same hundred people in the room want different rigs, because in one the bass supports the music and in the other the bass is the music. For those genres we add subwoofers or move to a larger box rather than pushing a small rig harder, since a speaker working at its limit stops sounding deep and starts sounding compressed. If low end is the whole point of the night, the BASSBOSS subwoofer rental page goes into more depth on sizing it.
### Not sure which line you are on?
Send us the venue name, the date and a rough head count. We know most DFW rooms, and for a new one we will ask for two photos and tell you honestly what it needs. That intake takes about five minutes and it decides whether the rig fits the room.

The Technology
## What a flat panel speaker is, and what makes the DML500 different
Panel Bending wave DML · carbon fiber and Nomex honeycomb · four neodymium motors · 165 degree coverage
A conventional loudspeaker moves air with a cone. A piston pushes forward and back, and the sound leaves the front of the box in a beam that gets narrower as the frequency rises. That is why a room covered by cone speakers has a loud spot in front of each one and a dull spot between them, and why the person sitting off to the side hears less of the top end than the person in the middle.
A flat panel speaker works on a different principle. Instead of a cone, it uses a stiff, light panel that is excited into bending waves across its whole surface. The panel moves in thousands of small modes at once. Thousands of small vibrational modes are spread across it at once, and the sound leaves as a diffuse wavefront rather than as a beam. In the Flat Panel Audio DML500 that panel is a carbon fiber and Nomex honeycomb composite, driven by four neodymium motor structures, inside an enclosure slim enough to hang like a picture frame.
The practical result is 165 degrees of horizontal coverage that stays intelligible right out to the edges. Speech holds together in a room where a cone box would be beaming past half the audience, and the level falls off far more gently as you walk away from it, so the front row stays comfortable while the level reaches the back row. It is a PA speaker, so it carries a program at real event levels rather than being a decorative background music panel.
Sound equipment rental
Audio services
Panel Versus Cone
## Low-profile panel speakers compared with the visual footprint of a speaker on a stick
Four differences that decide whether a flat panel loudspeaker is the right call for your room. Each one points to a specific set of jobs a panel does well, and we will tell you honestly whether yours is one of them.
01
### Coverage across the room
Panel 165 degrees horizontal · diffuse wavefront
A cone speaker narrows as frequency rises, so the seats off axis lose consonants first. The panel spreads a diffuse field across 165 degrees, which keeps speech readable at the sides of a room from the same panel. In a wide, shallow room that is often the difference between one flat panel and a pair of boxes on stands.
02
### How the level drops with distance
Panel Gentler falloff · smaller front to back spread
A point source loses roughly six decibels every time the distance doubles, which is why the first two rows get hammered so the last two rows can hear. The panel's falloff is gentler, so the range between the nearest listener and the furthest one is narrower. A gallery talk stays comfortable at the front and audible at the back off one system.
03
### A low-profile panel that hangs like a picture frame
Panel Low-profile enclosure · wall mount, stand or ground stack
This is the reason most people call about it. The DML500 is a thin panel that can sit flat against a wall or on a low-profile base, instead of a black trapezoid on a tripod at head height. In a room that has been styled by a designer, or photographed for a brand, a speaker with the footprint of a picture frame is worth a lot.
04
### Where a cone speaker still wins
Panel Add subwoofers for music and dancing
A flat panel is a mid and high device. It covers speech and background music beautifully; a dance floor, a live band or a rave wants a subwoofer alongside it. Pair it with subwoofers and it covers music well. For a DJ set, a band or a party where the bass is the point, we will say so and quote you a conventional rig instead.

## Panel speakers for events in rooms that will not take a speaker on a stick
The call almost always starts the same way: the venue, the designer or the client wants every speaker out of sight, and somebody still has to be heard. These are the rooms where that comes up in Dallas-Fort Worth, and what we do in each one.
### Museums and galleriesOpenings, donor events, curator talks
The art is the reason people are in the room, and a speaker on a tripod in front of a hung work is a problem before anybody turns it on. Flat panels go against a wall or on low-profile bases below sightline, cover the floor evenly for a talk that moves around the space, and come down with every wall surface untouched. Conservation staff care about what gets rigged and where, and we advance that with them rather than arriving with a plan.
### Historic venues and houses of worshipStone, glass, long reverb
Older rooms are difficult speech environments and they are rarely willing to be rigged. Hard stone and glass keep energy in the room long after the word has finished, so a beamy speaker pointed at the ceiling turns a sermon into mush. A diffuse panel field puts less energy into the reflective surfaces overhead and more into the seated area, which is why intelligibility comes up in the same room. Where a wireless microphone is in play, our AI-powered De-Feedback system runs on every channel, which is what buys usable gain in a room that wants to ring.
### Corporate rooms with sightline rulesProduct launches, showrooms, press
A launch stage gets designed months before anyone asks where the audio goes, and the answer is usually that there is nowhere for it. Flat panels sit inside a set, against a back wall or flanking a screen at a height below the camera line. For anything being filmed or streamed, that matters twice, because a speaker in shot is a speaker in the recording that goes on the company's channel afterward.
### Upscale retail and hospitalityTrunk shows, activations, hotel salons
Retail activations and hotel function rooms are styled to within an inch of their lives and are usually small enough that a full PA is overkill. A panel or a pair covers the space for a host, a short program and background music, tucks against a wall out of the traffic pattern, and reads as part of the room rather than as gear that showed up.
### Weddings at venues that ban visible speakersCeremonies, chapels, garden rooms
A growing number of DFW wedding venues have a written rule about visible black boxes in the ceremony space, and the aisle photograph is the reason. Flat panels solve the picture and the coverage at once: even level across seating that is wider than it is deep, a clean frame, and the officiant's wireless microphone running through the same system. Reception audio is a separate conversation, because the dance floor needs low end, which is a subwoofer's job.
### Conference breakouts and panel sessionsMeetings, seminars, training rooms
Breakout rooms are wide, low ceilinged and full of people sitting well off center. That geometry suits a flat panel and gives a pair of tops on sticks trouble. Panels along the front wall give the whole room the same intelligibility, and the presenter hears their own voice arrive on time.

## Flat panel speaker questions
What is a flat panel speaker?
A flat panel speaker replaces the cone of a conventional loudspeaker with a stiff, light panel that is excited into bending waves across its whole surface. Thousands of small vibrational modes spread across the panel at once, so the sound leaves as a diffuse wavefront rather than as a beam. That gives wide, even coverage from a thin enclosure that can sit flat against a wall. The Flat Panel Audio DML500 uses a carbon fiber and Nomex honeycomb panel driven by four neodymium motor structures, and covers 165 degrees horizontally.
How is the DML500 different from a regular PA speaker?
Three ways that matter on an event. Coverage is much wider and stays intelligible off to the sides, where a cone speaker narrows as frequency rises. Level drops off more gently with distance, so the front row is not overwhelmed to reach the back row. And the enclosure is a thin panel rather than a box on a tripod at head height, which is why it gets specified in rooms that have been designed or photographed. The trade is low end: a panel is a mid and high device and wants a subwoofer under it for music.
Can you use flat panel speakers for a live event, or are they only for background music?
They run live events. The DML500 is a PA speaker, so it carries speech and program material at real event levels rather than sitting at background volume. We use panels for gallery openings, donor events, curator talks, wedding ceremonies, product launches, worship services, breakout sessions and press conferences. For a dance floor or a live band we add subwoofers, or we quote a conventional system instead and tell you why.
Why do flat panel speakers work better in reverberant rooms?
Hard stone, glass and plaster hold sound energy in the room long after the word is finished, and a beamy speaker aimed into those surfaces feeds the problem. A diffuse panel field puts a larger share of its energy into the seated area and less into the reflective surfaces overhead, so more of what a listener hears is direct sound and less is reverberant wash. Intelligibility comes up without the room being changed, which is the only option in a building nobody is allowed to alter.
Our venue does not allow visible speakers. Does this solve that?
Usually, yes, and it is the usual reason people call us about panels. The DML500 is thin enough to sit flat against a wall or on a low-profile base below sightline, so the aisle photograph and the camera shot stay clear of speaker stands, and the visual clutter in the room is close to nothing. Send us the venue's rule in writing along with a photo of the room, and we will confirm before you book whether panels satisfy it or whether the venue is asking for something else entirely.
How many flat panels does a room need?
It comes from the shape of the room and where people are sitting, not from the guest count on its own. A wide, shallow room often needs fewer panels than you would expect, because 165 degrees of coverage from one position reaches seats that would need a second cone speaker aimed at them. A long, narrow room or a space with an obstruction in the middle needs more. Send the room and the seating plan and we will tell you what covers it.

De-Feedback
## Every open microphone is one step from feedback.
It shows up at the big moments: the officiant leaning in, the award winner turning to hug someone, the panelist gesturing with the handheld, the speaker stepping in front of the speakers.
Our AI-powered De-Feedback system runs on every microphone we rent, included in the rental. It listens for the ring before it becomes a squeal and takes that frequency out, which means your speakers can move the way people naturally move instead of being coached to stand on a piece of tape.
It matters more than it used to. Rooms with a stream or a recording run hotter, because the same microphones feed the PA and the broadcast, and that is the condition that makes an untreated system ring. This is also why we would rather set the microphone up ourselves than hand it over: the suppression is running on our system, tuned for your room.
The clip above walks through what the system is watching for. The waveform runs clean, one frequency finds the loop and rings up, the level meter climbs into the red, and then the suppression takes that frequency out and the voice keeps all of its tone.

At a recent ceremony in a downtown Dallas garden that was two lapel microphones, two EV ZLX speakers placed for the rows of chairs, and a condenser microphone over the string quartet so the prelude reached the last row. Wind is the real enemy outdoors, so the capsules get proper screening and we set levels with someone standing at the altar rather than at the mixer. See wedding audio .
### Reception & toastsBallroom or venue hall
Rig 2 wireless handhelds · reception system
Two wireless handhelds so one is always charged and in someone’s hand, plus the reception system doing double duty for music. Toasts are the microphone moment we plan hardest for at a wedding: people holding one for the first time, at their chest, in a room full of conversation. That is what the feedback suppression is for, along with a technician riding the level if you add one to the booking.
### Conference keynoteHotel ballroom or general session
Rig 1 headset or lapel · 1 podium · 2 handhelds on stands
A headset or lapel on the presenter, a podium microphone for introductions and a pair of handhelds on stands for floor questions, all mixed into a system that covers front-to-back evenly rather than blasting row one to reach row twenty. Add a confidence feed and the microphones for panels that follow. See corporate AV .
### Panel discussionStage or head table
Rig 1 mic per panelist · moderator mic · 1 roaming handheld
One microphone per panelist (lapels if they are on stools or standing, tabletop push-to-talk if they are seated at a table), plus a moderator microphone and at least one roaming handheld for the audience. Sharing microphones across a panel is a common reason a recorded panel is unusable afterwards.
### Board & committee meetingBoard room or council chamber
Rig push-to-talk tabletop, one per seat · clean feed out
Push-to-talk tabletop microphones, one per seat, so the minutes are clean and the remote attendees hear a person instead of a room. We set the coverage so everyone can sit back, and we can send a clean feed straight into whatever platform the meeting is on. Pairs naturally with live streaming .
### Worship serviceSanctuary or multipurpose room
Rig 1 headset · handhelds · podium · choir and instrument coverage
A headset on the pastor, handhelds and a podium microphone for readings and announcements, and instrument or choir coverage for the music team. Sanctuaries are hard rooms: hard surfaces, high ceilings, microphones a long way in front of the speakers. That is where the feedback suppression matters most.
### Press conferencePodium or step-and-repeat
Rig 1 podium mic · press feed · handhelds for questions
A podium microphone plus a press feed so every outlet in the room pulls clean audio from the same source instead of stacking a dozen recorders on the lectern. Handhelds for questions from the floor, so the answer makes sense on the recording.
### Live band or ensembleVenue, campus or outdoor stage
Rig full input list · stage monitoring
A full input list covering drums, amps, acoustic instruments and vocals, with monitoring so the band can hear themselves, mixed by someone who has done it before. Send the stage plot and we will build to it. See live music events .

Questions
## What people ask before they book microphones.
Can I rent just a microphone on its own?
We quote it as a speaker and microphone rental, because microphones go out as part of a full sound system. A microphone does not make anyone louder by itself: the speaker, the mixer and the setup do that. Bundling them is also what lets us guarantee it works when the room fills, because we tuned the whole chain together. More on sound system rental .
What kinds of microphones do you carry?
Wireless handhelds, lapel and lavalier microphones on bodypacks, over-the-ear headsets, gooseneck podium and lectern microphones, push-to-talk tabletop microphones for conference and board rooms, and instrument, choir and overhead microphones for bands and worship teams. Most events use a combination, and working out that combination is part of the quote.
What is the AI De-Feedback system?
It is feedback suppression that runs on every microphone we rent, standard. It identifies the frequency that is about to ring and removes it before the room hears a squeal, which lets speakers move naturally instead of being told to stay behind a line. It is running on our system, tuned for your room, which is one of the reasons we set the microphones up ourselves.
What is included in a rental?
We deliver, build, ring out, line-check and strike everything ourselves, and we sound check with your DJ or presenter before doors. A technician can stay on site to run the microphones for the event on request, and for complex setups we recommend one.
How many microphones do I need for a panel?
One per panelist, plus a moderator microphone and at least one roaming handheld for audience questions. Panelists sharing a microphone is a common reason a recorded panel turns out unusable, and it slows the discussion down in the room as well.
Do you have microphones for a podium or lectern?
Yes. Gooseneck microphones that mount to a lectern, and stand-mounted podium microphones where there is nothing to mount to. We aim it and set it with someone standing at it, which is the step most podium setups skip. Every microphone we send out includes the De-Feedback system, so there is no ringing out involved and the podium holds up once the room fills.
Can everyone at the board table have their own microphone?
Yes. For board meetings, council sessions, committee hearings and hybrid meeting rooms we set push-to-talk tabletop microphones, one per seat, live only while the button is held. That keeps a table of open microphones from picking up shuffling papers and side conversations, and it gives you a clean feed for the recording or the stream.
Do you have lapel and headset microphones?
Both, on wireless bodypacks. Lapel and lavalier microphones are the standard for officiants, panelists and anyone being filmed; headsets hold a consistent distance from the mouth and hold gain better, which makes them the right answer for long presentations, instructors and worship leaders. We place them on the person rather than handing them over in a bag.
Will a wireless microphone work outdoors?
Yes, and outdoor ceremonies are a large share of what we do. Outdoors the issues are wind and coverage rather than feedback, so capsules get proper screening and the system is placed to cover the seating area rather than the open field behind it. We also bring power solutions for sites without a convenient outlet.
What areas of Dallas-Fort Worth do you serve?
The whole Metroplex: roughly a forty-mile radius from the mid-cities, covering Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, Frisco, Irving, Southlake, McKinney, Richardson, Grapevine, Denton and everywhere in between. If your venue is further out, ask anyway and we will tell you honestly whether it works.

Send the date, the venue and roughly how many people, and we’ll send you a straightforward quote within 24 hours.

How To Read This
## How the equipment list works
This page is the inventory behind every quote we send. It is here so you can see what we own before you call, and so you can tell whether we are the right company for the event you are planning. Each category links to the page that goes into detail on it.
Everything ships as a production package. We deliver it to your venue, build it inside the load-in window, dress the cabling, line-check it and tune it to the room, then strike it afterward, and a technician stays on it for the event on the services that call for one. Placement, gain structure and a line check in the room are what decide whether a room sounds right, and all of that travels with the crew rather than in a road case.
You will notice this page lists families rather than counts. Our inventory turns over as we buy, sell and replace boxes, and a number printed here would be out of date within a season. FAQ
## Equipment list questions
Can I rent one item from the equipment list on its own?
CDJs and DJ mixers are the exception, and they rent on their own: delivered, set up and sound checked with your DJ, then picked up after the event. Everything else on this list goes out as part of a package that includes delivery, setup, testing and pickup, with an operator on the services that call for one, because a single microphone or light rarely justifies a delivery and a setup by itself. Tell us about the event and we will put together the smallest package that covers it.
What is included in a rental?
Delivery, setup, tuning and collection are included. We deliver to the venue, build the system inside the load-in window, tune it to the room, test it and take it away afterward, and a technician runs it for the event on the services that call for one. Your team does not touch a cable at any point in that.
Why are there no quantities on this equipment list?
Because our inventory turns over as we buy, sell and replace boxes, so a number printed on a web page would be out of date within a season. We size the rig to your room on the quote instead. The one exception is the line array, where the shape is fixed: BassBoss DV12-MK3 cabinets, up to two a side on heavy duty stands, over a BassBoss subwoofer array. That is part of what you are comparing when you get line array quotes.
Do you own this equipment or sub-rent it?
We own it. The system that arrives has been used by our crew in rooms like yours, including the line array, its audio crew and the stands it goes up on, so we already know how it behaves when a venue's power is not what the floor plan promised. The two exceptions are LED video wall, which we coordinate through vendors we work with regularly, and large CO2 cylinders, which come from a gas supplier. We tell you which is which on the quote.
Do you rent inflatable or outdoor movie screens?
No. We do not carry inflatable screens or outdoor movie screens in any size. Our projection equipment is built for indoor and covered spaces where we can control the ambient light, including an ambient light rejecting screen for rooms that cannot be made dark.
What if the equipment I need is not on this list?

Do you deliver across Dallas-Fort Worth?

Yes, on the services that call for one (DJ, live sound, corporate and streaming) and whenever you ask. When a technician stays, the person who tuned the system in the afternoon is the person behind it in the evening.

What Full Service Means
## Four things have to happen. Most companies do one of them.
Plenty of outfits will put lighting fixtures on a truck. The gap between that and an event that looks designed is the other three steps, and they are the ones that decide whether the room works.
01
### Design
We start from your venue, your colors and the moments that matter: the entrance, the first dance, the keynote, the award. The plan comes from the room’s actual dimensions and surfaces, not from a package tier.
02
### Install
We deliver, place, rig, cable and focus everything ourselves, working to the venue’s load-in window and rules. Certificates of insurance go to your venue ahead of time so the dock opens on time.
03
### Operate, react or program
Follow spot and laser shows get a technician who stays for the whole event and runs them live, and moving lights and anything cued to the show can have a lighting engineer as an option. The follow spot finds the couple, and with an engineer on the show the stage wash comes up when the speaker does. DJ and dance floor lighting is aimed and set to sound reactive mode as standard, so it follows the music on its own, with a lighting engineer available on request to run the looks live from a lighting console on the more involved rigs. Uplighting and monogram projection are programmed at load-in, with colors and changes set against your run sheet so they hold on their own. Where a technician is already on site for another part of your booking, they can take the programmed fixtures live as well.
04
### Strike
We break it all down and pack it out at the end, on the venue’s schedule. Our crew coils the cable and loads it out at the end of the night.
There is no pickup option. Every job we take is designed, installed, operated or programmed on site, and struck by our own crew, and that is the only way we work. Even the fixtures that run themselves are placed, color matched, focused and programmed by us, and we come back for them at the end.
Every Type We Do
## The lighting, one type at a time.
Most events use three or four of these together. Tell us the venue and what happens in it and we will tell you which ones earn their place, and which ones you can skip.
The Room
### Uplighting & color wash
Battery-powered wireless fixtures around the perimeter, washing walls, columns, drape and architecture in your colors. Uplighting changes the whole room at once, and it changes every photograph taken that night. We place it, color match it and program the look at load-in, including any changes across the evening, and it runs to your run sheet from there. Our crew returns afterward to strike it.
Best for Ballrooms, barns, tents, atriums, historic halls, and anywhere the walls are doing nothing for you.
The Floor
### Dance floor & DJ lighting
Moving heads, wash fixtures and effects focused on the floor, sized to the dance floor rather than the room. It runs sound reactive by default, so the fixtures follow the music on their own while we deliver, aim, set the mode and come back after the event to strike. Ask and we will put a lighting engineer on it to run the looks live, and on the more involved rigs that engineer runs a lighting console. A floor lit like a nightclub in a room of eighty reads as too much, and we would rather say so than sell it. More on DJ and dance floor lighting .
Best for Receptions, private parties, quinceañeras, school and college events, club nights.
Fixtures That Move
### Moving heads & intelligent lighting
Motorized fixtures that pan, tilt, change color and shape their beam on command, so one light does the work of six and the room keeps moving. They are what makes a dance floor feel programmed rather than switched on, and they are also the quiet workhorse of a corporate general session. The same fixture that throws a beam across a club can re-focus onto a lectern between segments. Ours are programmed to your timeline at load-in, and for a show with live cues a lighting engineer can operate them from the room.
Best for Dance floors, club and rave nights, concerts and festivals, award shows, general sessions, product reveals.
Faces, Not Silhouettes
### Stage & ceremony wash
Front light on the people being watched: the couple at the altar, the band, the keynote, the award recipient. Rooms are almost always lit from above and behind, which flatters the ceiling and ruins faces on camera. A wash from the front is what makes the video worth keeping.
Best for Ceremonies, live bands, keynotes, panels, awards, anything filmed or streamed.
Your Name, Ten Feet Tall
### Monogram & gobo projection
A custom monogram, initials, date, logo or pattern projected onto a wall, a dance floor or a ceiling. We cut the gobo from your artwork and focus it on site so it stays sharp from the back of the room. Corporate events use the identical fixture for a company or sponsor logo. It is set at load-in and holds its look for the night, and our crew comes back to strike it.
Best for Wedding dance floors, sponsor walls, brand activations, award nights.
Precision
### Pin spot lighting
Tight narrow beams aimed at one thing each: centerpieces, the cake, the head table, an escort card display. Pin spots are why the flowers you paid a florist for still read as flowers once the house lights come down, instead of vanishing into a dim table.
Best for Centerpieces, cake tables, head and sweetheart tables, product and trophy displays.
One Person, All Eyes
### Follow spot
A live-operated beam that tracks one person across a room: the grand entrance, the first dance, the speaker walking to the lectern, the artist working the stage. It depends entirely on the person running it, which is why it goes out with an operator.
Best for Grand entrances, first dances, keynotes, awards, theater and concert work.
The Big Swing
### Laser shows & specialty effects
Full laser systems for events that want the room to go somewhere else entirely, plus low-lying fog for a dancing-on-the-clouds first dance. These make a moment rather than a room. They earn their keep on one or two cues rather than across four hours.
Best for Grand reveals, first dances, after-parties, club nights, festivals, brand launches.
Rooms That Work For A Living
### Meeting room & architectural lighting
Conference rooms, board rooms, ballroom general sessions and breakouts, lit so the room reads as considered on camera and people can still see their notes. A common corporate lighting problem is a room lit for a hotel lobby and used for a keynote: too flat, too warm, and the presenter in shadow.
Best for Conferences, board and council meetings, general sessions, hybrid and streamed meetings, training.

One Vendor
## Event lighting and sound, from the same crew.
Most of our events are both. Running them together is the reason the cues land. When the same team runs the lighting console and the audio, the room goes dark on the right beat, the wash comes up as the speaker is introduced rather than eight seconds after, and the first dance lighting starts when the song does.
It also removes an entire category of event-day problem: one load-in, one crew, one certificate of insurance, one person your planner has to call. One crew on the stage means one setup in the dock window and one person who owns the overlap.
Where there are microphones involved, our systems run AI-powered De-Feedback on every one of them. It identifies the frequency about to ring and removes it before the room hears a squeal, so a presenter can move naturally instead of being told to stay behind a line. There is a plain explanation of how it works if you want the detail.

Lighting Design
## What a lighting designer is deciding.
This is the part a rental list leaves out, and it is most of what separates a room that looks designed from a room that looks lit. Every one of these gets settled before a fixture goes on the truck.
### The surfaces worth lightingAnd the ones worth leaving alone
Columns, beams, drape, brick and a coffered ceiling all repay light. A stained ceiling tile, a service door, a stack of banquet chairs are left in the dark on purpose. Half of a good plan is choosing what stays dark.
### Fixture count and spacingMeasured, not guessed
Coverage comes from wall length and beam angle, not guest count or square footage. Spaced too far apart and you get scallops of light with dark gaps between them, which reads as cheap even to people who could not tell you why.
### What the house lights are doingThe hidden variable
Venue house lighting is a common reason a lighting plan underdelivers. We find out early what can be dimmed, what is on a locked panel, what the staff will agree to turn down, and design to the level you will really have.
### The timeline, cue by cueWhere the changes go
Doors, ceremony, dinner, toasts, first dance, open floor and last song each want something different. We map lighting states to your run of show so the room shifts with the night instead of sitting on one look for six hours.
### How it photographsPlanned for the camera as well as the eye
Deeply saturated blues and magentas look striking to the eye and can wreck skin tones in a photograph. We coordinate with your photographer and videographer, and we will tell you when a color you love needs to live on the far wall rather than behind the head table.
### Power, rigging and venue rulesThe unglamorous part
Where circuits are, what can be rigged, whether fixtures need to be battery powered because the nearest outlet is across the room, what the fire marshal and the venue coordinator will sign off on. Sorted before the day, not discovered on it.
Corporate & Meetings
## Conference and meeting room lighting that reads on camera.
A general session, a board meeting and a gala are three different lighting problems, and each needs its own design on top of the hotel house lighting. At a Christmas holiday party last year we held the company's cyan across the room through the presentations, then took the whole perimeter to red and green when the program ended and the mingling started. The usual starting point is a room lit flat and warm from overhead: the presenter in shadow, the screen washed out, and everyone on the stream looking tired.
We front-light the stage or lectern so faces are properly exposed for the room, the cameras and the recording; we bring the ambient level down enough that the screen has contrast while the audience can still see the dark; and we wash the room in your brand colors, matched from your actual hex values rather than the closest preset. Logo gobo projection beside the stage uses the same fixture a wedding monogram does.
For hybrid and streamed meetings this matters even more. A camera has far less latitude than an eye, and it shows every shadow on a speaker lit from directly above.

Outdoor & Tented
## Outdoor event lighting is a different problem entirely.
Texas outdoor events are won or lost on lighting more often than on anything else, and almost always for the same three reasons.
### Power has to come with you
Ranches, estates, parks and open fields rarely have power where the lighting needs to be. Battery-powered fixtures and properly planned distribution mean the plan holds together far from the nearest outlet.
### Trees and tent poles become the walls
Uplighting needs a surface. Outdoors that means trees, hedges, a building facade, tent poles and peaks, or an entrance arch, and the plan has to be built around what is there rather than a ballroom layout moved outside.
### The sun sets in the middle of it
An outdoor event changes lighting conditions completely halfway through. We plan for the ceremony in daylight and the reception in the dark, and for the forty minutes in between, which get their own plan.
### Weather is part of the plan
Fixture ratings, covered positions and a plan for wind and rain, agreed before the day. DFW weather turns fast enough that the plan has to be made before the day.

Questions
## Event lighting, answered plainly.
Do you do lighting design, or just deliver the equipment?
Design first, always. We work out the plan for your specific venue (surfaces, fixture count, color, cue timing, power and rigging) as part of quoting the job, then we install it, program it to your run sheet and strike it. Lasers and follow spot are run live by our technician, and a lighting engineer is available for the more complex rigs. There is no version of this where fixtures arrive and someone on your side works out where they go.
Can I book lighting only, without a DJ or sound?
Yes, and we do it regularly. If you already have a DJ, a band or in-house AV, we supply the lighting and coordinate with them directly on cues and timing. Most of our events are lighting and sound together because the cues line up better that way, but it is not a requirement.
What is included in a rental?
We deliver, place, rig, focus, program and strike everything ourselves. Follow spot and laser shows get a technician on site for the whole event, and a lighting engineer is available as an option for moving lights and anything cued to the show. DJ and dance floor lighting runs sound reactive by default, so we deliver it, aim it, set the mode and come back after the event to strike, and a lighting engineer is available on request to run the looks live. Uplighting and monogram projection are programmed to your run sheet at load-in and hold on their own, and our crew comes back afterward to strike them. Where a technician is already on site for another part of your booking, they can take those fixtures live as well. We deliver, place and collect every fixture ourselves. Programming lighting in the actual room, with the house lights at the level you will really have, is most of what makes it look designed rather than rented.
How far in advance should I book event lighting?
Earlier is better, particularly for Saturdays in spring and fall and anywhere in December. That said, we would always rather you asked late than not at all. Tell us the date and we will tell you straight away whether we have the crew and the fixtures free.
Can you match our brand colors?
Yes. Send hex values from your brand guidelines, a swatch or a photograph and we will match it. We will also tell you honestly what that color does in your particular room, because a shade that is perfect on screen can read very differently washed across a wall, and it is better to adjust it with you standing in the room than to have you see it for the first time at the event.
Do you light conference rooms and board meetings?
Yes, and it is a meaningful part of what we do. Meeting rooms, board and council chambers, general sessions and breakouts all get lit for the camera as much as the room: proper front light on whoever is presenting, an ambient level that leaves the screen readable, and none of the flat overhead wash that makes everyone on a stream look exhausted.
Will lighting work at an outdoor or tented venue?
Yes, with a different plan. Outdoors the power is usually somewhere else and the walls are missing, so we work with battery fixtures and light what is there: trees, a facade, tent poles and peaks, an entrance. We also plan for the light changing completely partway through the evening, which is the step most outdoor setups skip.
Our venue has its own lighting. Do we still need you?
Sometimes not, and we will say so. House lighting is generally built to make a room usable rather than to make it look like anything, and it is rarely dimmable in the way an event needs. Tell us the venue and we will tell you what its lighting genuinely does, including when the honest answer is that you need less from us than you thought.
Do you work with our planner, photographer and videographer?
Directly, and we prefer it. Lighting affects every one of them. The photographer cares about color temperature and where the saturated tones sit, the videographer cares about front light and flicker, the planner cares about load-in windows. Being in that conversation early prevents nearly every lighting problem we have seen turn up on an event day.
What areas of Dallas-Fort Worth do you cover?
The whole Metroplex: roughly a forty-mile radius from the mid-cities, covering Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, Frisco, Irving, Southlake, McKinney, Richardson, Grapevine, Denton and everywhere in between. If your venue is further out, ask anyway and we will tell you honestly whether it works.

## Mix an uplighting color on a virtual wall.
Our uplights hold six colors of LED behind one lens: red, green, blue, white, amber and UV. The color that lands on your wall is all six of them adding together. Move the faders the way a technician does at load in, change the surface you are aiming at, and watch what the room gives back.

### White and amber are what make pastels possible
Red, green and blue on their own give you saturated color. White lifts a saturated color toward a pastel, which is how blush, ice blue and champagne happen at all. Amber warms skin tones and keeps a room from looking like a computer monitor.
### The UV fader looks broken until you aim it at white
UV puts out very little visible light of its own. Point it at white drape, linens or shirts carrying optical brightener and the fabric starts glowing. Set the surface to white drape and push UV up by itself to see it.
### The wall decides half of the color
The same fader positions land differently on white drape, on a gray ballroom wall and on brick, because a wall reflects only what it already contains. Deep blue on brick nearly disappears. That is why we walk your venue before we promise a color, and why we set color on site rather than from a swatch emailed ahead of time.
### A real room adds light of its own
This is a simulation, built for the fun of it. House lights, candles, window light at golden hour and whatever your photographer is bouncing off the ceiling all move the answer, which is what the walkthrough on the day of your event is for.

Wedding Uplighting
## Uplighting changes the entire room at once.
Every venue looks like itself under the house lights. Beige walls stay beige, the ceiling stays wherever it is, and the photos come back looking like a conference room with flowers in it. Uplighting is what turns that room into your room: a ring of lights around the perimeter, aimed up the walls and columns, washing the whole space in a color you chose.
It is the first thing we recommend on most wedding lighting lists, because it works on the whole space rather than one corner of it, and every photograph taken that night is taken in the light you chose. It also does something few people think to ask for: it pulls the eye up the walls, away from a dated carpet, a service door or a wall of banquet chairs stacked in the corner.
We place them the afternoon of your event, walk the room with the color up, and adjust until the wash is even. Then we come back at the end of the night and take them out. Every fixture is ours to handle.
At a Halloween themed wedding last fall we set the perimeter in amber and orange, alternating fixture by fixture, and programmed them to fade slowly up and down in intensity so the whole room flickered like candlelight. The photographs look like the reception was lit by a hundred candles, and every one of them was a battery uplight on the floor.

Uplighting In Detail
## Where the uplights go.
“Uplighting” sounds like one thing you either have or do not have. In practice it is six or seven separate decisions about surfaces, and the difference between a room that looks designed and a room that looks lit is which of them somebody thought about.
The Base Layer
### Perimeter wall wash
Fixtures spaced evenly around the outside of the room, aimed straight up the walls. This is what people mean when they say uplighting, and it is the layer everything else sits on top of. Spacing is the whole game. Too far apart and you get scallops of light with dark gaps between them, which reads as cheap even to people who could not tell you why.
Watch for Long unbroken walls, which need more fixtures than their square footage suggests.
Structure
### Columns, arches & architectural detail
Columns, pilasters, archways, alcoves, beams and stone detail are the features that a venue was designed around, and house lighting almost always flattens them. A fixture at the base of a column throws light and shadow up its full height. It is the same trick used on buildings at night, and it gives a flat banquet room vertical depth.
Watch for Historic venues, hotel ballrooms with pilasters, barns with exposed posts and trusses.
The Photo Wall
### Drape, backdrop & head table
The wall behind the head table, the sweetheart table or the stage is in a disproportionate number of your photographs, so it gets treated separately from the rest of the perimeter. Washing drape from below gives fabric its folds back; a flat wall behind a couple reads better in a slightly different tone from the rest of the room, so they separate from it rather than disappearing into it.
Watch for Head tables, sweetheart tables, stages, step-and-repeat and sponsor walls.
Where People Stand
### Bars, lounges & cocktail spaces
Cocktail hour and the bar area are usually lit by whatever the venue happens to have, which is usually the house lights alone. Uplighting a bar front, a lounge grouping or a cocktail area carries your color into the parts of the night that happen before and around dinner, so the evening looks like one event rather than a lit room and some corridors.
Watch for Separate cocktail rooms, foyers, pre-function space, outdoor patios.
Outside
### Outdoor & facade uplighting
Trees, hedges, a building facade, a tent’s poles and peaks, the entrance guests walk through. Outdoor uplighting is what stops an evening event from ending at the doorway, and it is the first thing arriving guests see. It is also a power, weather and fixture-rating conversation before it is a design one, which is where battery fixtures earn their keep.
Watch for Tented receptions, ranch and estate venues, entrances, outdoor ceremonies.
Overhead
### Ceilings & structure
In rooms with something worth showing overhead (a coffered ceiling, exposed trusses, a tent’s interior peak) light aimed up into it lifts the whole space and makes a low room feel taller. Where the ceiling is plain, we leave it dark and let the walls carry the room.
Watch for Tents, barns, atriums, historic halls, anywhere with height going unused.
How An Uplighting Plan Is Built
## The six things we work out before a single fixture is loaded.
This is the part a rental listing leaves out, and it is most of what you are paying someone for.
### Spacing and fixture countMeasured, not guessed
We work from the room’s actual wall lengths and lay fixtures out so their beams overlap slightly before they reach the top of the wall. That overlap is what produces an unbroken wash instead of a row of separate glowing patches. The math decides it, and it is the first thing we check in any uplighting plan.
### Wall height and beam angleHow far the light travels
A ten-foot banquet room wall and a twenty-four-foot barn wall need different beam angles to fill properly. Too narrow and the color stops a third of the way up; too wide and it spills across the ceiling. We ask about ceiling height early because it changes the fixture choice as well as the count.
### Battery runtime versus your timelineFrom doors to last dance
Wireless fixtures run on their own batteries, which means runtime has to cover your whole event with margin, including the ceremony, the photos before doors, and the reception running long, which it usually does. We plan to the real length of your night rather than the four hours on the contract.
### Fixed color or programmed changesOne look or several
The simplest version is one color set at load-in that holds all night. The better version, in most rooms, changes: warm and low through dinner, then something with more energy when the floor opens. Our technician programs that sequence into presets before doors open, and your DJ or planner recalls each one with a single button press, so the room follows the night. Color changes called by hand during the event are available with a lighting engineer on request, and a technician already on site for your audio, a follow spot or a fuller production package with us can call them too.
### What the house lights are doingThe hidden variable
Uplighting competes with whatever the venue has on its own dimmers. A ballroom at full house level will wash out any color you put on the walls. Part of our job is knowing which venues can dim and who to talk to about it before the day, because a room that keeps its house lights up needs a different design.
### How it photographsPlanned for the camera as well as the eye
Cameras and eyes disagree. Saturated blues and magentas look striking in the room and can cool skin tones in every photo taken in front of them. We plan colors that hold up in both, coordinate with your photographer or videographer when they have preferences, and tell you when the color you want will not be kind to your photographs.
Pairs Well With
## What we usually pair with the uplights.
Uplighting sets the room, but most nights want two or three of these working together. Tell us the venue and what is happening in it and we will tell you which ones matter, or see the full range on our lighting services page.
Color Wash
### LED uplighting
Battery-powered wireless uplights placed around the perimeter of the room, washing the walls, columns, drapes and architectural features in a single color or a designed sequence. Everything runs on battery power, so your floor stays clear and so do the doorways your guests walk through.
Best for Ballrooms, receptions, barns, tents, atriums, and anywhere the walls are doing nothing for you.
The Floor
### Dance floor & DJ lighting
Moving heads, wash fixtures and effect lighting focused on the dance floor and run to the music, so the energy changes when the set does. Sized to the floor rather than the room. A dance floor lit like a nightclub in a room of eighty people reads as too much, and we would rather tell you that than sell it to you.
Best for Receptions, private parties, quinceañeras, school and college events, club nights.
Your Name, Ten Feet Tall
### Monogram & gobo projection
A custom monogram, initials, date, logo or pattern projected onto a wall, a dance floor or the ceiling. We cut the gobo from your artwork, focus it on site and keep it sharp from the back of the room. Corporate events use the same fixture for a logo beside the stage.
Best for Wedding dance floors, sponsor walls, brand activations, award nights.
Precision
### Pin spot lighting
Tight, narrow beams aimed at one thing each: the centerpieces, the cake, the head table, the escort card display. Pin spots are why the flowers you paid a florist for still read as flowers once the room goes dark, instead of disappearing into a dim table.
Best for Centerpieces, cake tables, head tables, sweetheart tables, displays.
Faces, Not Silhouettes
### Stage & ceremony wash
Front light on the people who are being watched: the couple at the altar, the band, the keynote speaker, the award recipient. Rooms are almost always lit from above and behind, which is flattering to the ceiling and ruinous to faces on camera. A wash from the front is what makes the video worth keeping.
Best for Ceremonies, live bands, keynotes, awards, anything being filmed or streamed.
The Big Moments
### Effects & specialty lighting
Follow spot for a grand entrance or a first dance, low-lying fog for a dancing-on-the-clouds first dance, and full laser shows for events that want the room to go somewhere else entirely. These make a moment rather than a room. They pay off on one or two cues rather than across the whole night.
Best for First dances, grand entrances, reveals, after-parties, club and rave nights.

Venue By Venue
## What uplighting does in a Dallas-Fort Worth venue like yours.
The same fixtures do very different things depending on the walls they are pointed at. This is the conversation we would have with you on a site visit.
### Hotel ballroomNeutral walls, low ceiling
The classic case. Beige or gray walls, patterned carpet, a ceiling full of house downlights that flatten everything. Uplighting around the perimeter replaces the room’s color entirely, and dropping the house lights once dinner is served is what makes it land. Ballrooms are also where an even wash matters most, because the walls are long and flat and show every gap.
### Barn & ranch venueWood, beams, height
Wood eats light, so barns need more fixtures than their square footage suggests, and warmer colors read far better than cool ones on stained timber. The win here is the vertical structure: posts, beams and trusses lit from below give the space a depth that bistro lights on their own only hint at.
### Historic & brickTexture worth showing
Exposed brick, stone and plaster are the one case where the wall is already the feature. Uplighting is aimed at raking across the surface rather than flooding it, so the texture throws its own shadows. Restrained color and more contrast, so the building is revealed rather than repainted. We lit a dim brick warehouse for a private event with pure white uplights and the room changed completely: the brick came forward, the ceiling gained height, and the space read as a venue instead of a storage floor.
### Country club & private diningWindows and warm wood
Lots of glass, which means the look changes completely between the cocktail hour and full dark. We plan for both, and we plan around the reflections, because an uplight aimed at a window wall at nine o’clock is lighting the parking lot.
### Tent & outdoor receptionPoles, peaks and drapes to wash
With open sides, the light goes somewhere else: up the tent poles and into the peaks, along the perimeter drapes, into the trees at the edge of the site. Outdoor lighting is also a power and weather conversation before it is a design conversation, and battery fixtures solve most of it.
### Church & chapelFixed lighting, high ceilings
Ceremony spaces usually have fixed house lighting and a venue that limits what may be attached to anything. The work is front light on the couple and gentle accents that respect the space, and coordinating early, because the venue’s rules decide this one.
Choosing Your Color
## Choosing an uplighting color that works in your room.
Clients usually arrive with a swatch from the florist or a screenshot from Pinterest, and the honest answer is that a color on fabric and the same color on a wall are two different colors. Deep jewel tones read rich in a large ballroom and heavy in a small one. Blush and champagne look beautiful in person and can vanish on camera. Sharp blues photograph dramatically but drain the warmth out of skin tones on the dance floor.
So we talk about it. Bring your palette, your venue and your photographer’s preferences, and we will tell you what that combination does in that room, including when the answer is a warmer version of what you asked for.
Colors can also change through the night: one tone for the ceremony, a second for dinner, something with more energy when the dancing starts. That is a programming decision we make once, and it lands on a button.
If you want to see how a color behaves on a given surface before you commit to it, mix one on the virtual wall at the top of this page and switch the surface underneath it.

Corporate & Brand Events
## Corporate event lighting in your brand colors.
The same fixtures that wash a wedding in blush will hold a brand color across a whole ballroom for a gala, a product launch, a sales kickoff or an awards night. Give us the hex value from your brand guidelines and we will match it and hold it consistently on every wall, which matters when the room is going to appear in the recap video and on your social feed. At a Christmas holiday party we held the company's cyan across the room through the presentations, then shifted the whole perimeter to red and green when the program ended and the mingling started, so the brand had the stage and the season had the party.
Add a gobo of the company logo or a sponsor mark beside the stage, a proper front wash so your executives are lit rather than silhouetted, and it stops looking like a hotel function room. If there is a stage, a panel or a presentation involved, lighting and audio should be quoted together, and every microphone we send out runs our AI-powered De-Feedback system, so a speaker can walk the stage and the sound stays clean.

Planning Your Budget
## What drives the size of an uplighting quote.
Every quote is built for the room, because the same package lands differently in a long ballroom and a compact square one. What we can do is tell you honestly what moves it, so you know what you are trading when you plan.
### Wall length before guest countThe main driver
Uplighting is priced by how much wall there is rather than how many people are in front of it. A long narrow ballroom for a hundred guests can need more fixtures than a compact square room for two hundred. This is why we ask about the venue before anything else.
### How many elements you addUplights, floor, monogram, pins
Uplighting on its own is the entry point. Dance floor lighting, a monogram, pin spots on the centerpieces and a ceremony wash are each separate additions. Most rooms do well with two or three of them, and we will tell you which ones make the biggest difference to yours.
### Load-in conditionsAccess, timing, stairs
A venue with a loading dock and a four-hour window is a different job from a third-floor historic room with a service elevator and a ninety-minute turn between events. Tell us early and the quote covers it from the start.
### Whether we are already thereBundling with audio or DJ
If we are handling your sound system, your DJ or your AV, the lighting shares the same trip, the same crew and the same setup. Booking it together is more efficient than adding it to a separate vendor’s invoice.
### The honest version
Send us the date, the venue name and roughly how many guests, and you will have a real quote back, with the fixture count and the plan for your room spelled out in it. If uplighting alone is the right call for your room, we will say so rather than talking you up.
