Questions
## Uplighting rental, answered plainly.
How many uplights does my room need?
It comes from the length of your walls, not your guest count. We space fixtures so the wash overlaps rather than leaving scallops of light with dark gaps between them, and long rooms need more than their square footage suggests. Send us the venue name and we will work it out from their floor plan. We have been in most Dallas-Fort Worth venues already.
Do the uplights need to be plugged in?
They run the whole event on their own batteries. Our uplights are wireless, so they can be placed anywhere in the room, including against a wall with the nearest outlet across the room. That means your floor stays clear of cable and your guests walk through a clean doorway, which is also what most venues prefer.
Can you match a specific color?
Yes. Bring a swatch, a hex value from your brand guidelines or a photo, and we will match it. We will also be honest with you about what that color does in your particular room, because a shade that looks perfect on fabric can read very differently washed across a wall, and we would rather adjust it with you standing in the room than have you see it for the first time at the reception.
Can the colors change during the event?
Yes, and it is one of the better uses of the system. A warmer tone for the ceremony and dinner, then something with more energy when the dancing starts, is a common program. We build those changes into DMX presets at load-in, one button each, so your DJ or planner shifts the room with the night instead of leaving it on one color for six hours. Color changes called by hand are available with a lighting engineer, which you can add on request for more complex setups, and a technician already on site for your audio, a follow spot or a fuller production package with us can call them too.
Do you deliver and set up, or do I pick the lights up?
We deliver, place, aim, focus, program and strike everything ourselves, and our crew comes back after the event to take every fixture out. We deliver, place and collect every fixture ourselves. Setting the color in the actual room with the house lights at the actual level is most of what makes uplighting look designed rather than rented.
What is a monogram or gobo projector?
It is a focused light with a custom-cut pattern in it, projecting your initials, your names and date, a logo or a decorative design onto a wall, a dance floor or a ceiling. We cut the gobo from your artwork and focus it on site. Corporate clients use the same fixture for a company or sponsor logo beside the stage.
What are pin spots for?
Pin spots are narrow beams aimed at one object: a centerpiece, the cake, the head table, a display. Once the house lights come down for dancing, tall floral arrangements and a cake you spent real money on disappear into a dark table. Pin spots keep them visible and photographable all night.
Do you light the dance floor as well?
Yes. Moving heads, wash fixtures and effects focused on the floor and run to the music, sized to the dance floor rather than the room. It is a different job from uplighting: uplighting sets the mood of the whole space for the entire night, dance floor lighting drives energy in one area for part of it. Most receptions want both, and they should be designed together.
Can I book lighting and sound together?
That is how most of our events run. One vendor means one load-in, one crew, one point of contact and lighting cues that line up with the music, because the same team is running both. If you already have a DJ, we are happy to supply lighting only and coordinate with them directly.
What areas of Dallas-Fort Worth do you cover?
The whole Metroplex: roughly a forty-mile radius from the mid-cities, covering Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, Frisco, Irving, Southlake, McKinney, Richardson, Grapevine, Denton and everywhere in between. If your venue is further out, ask anyway and we will tell you honestly whether it works.

What DJ Lighting Is
## Dance floor lighting is a design built around one floor.
“DJ lighting” usually gets pictured as a couple of fixtures on sticks either side of a booth, flashing to the beat. That is the version most people have seen, and it is also the version that makes a room look smaller than it is. Real dance floor lighting is a rig aimed at a specific piece of floor, in a specific room, with the fixtures chosen for the ceiling height and the crowd size in front of them.
The difference is easy to see and hard to describe in a quote line. A designed rig has layers: something covering the floor in color, something cutting through the air above it, something adding texture on the walls, and haze to make any of it visible. Take one layer away and the whole thing flattens out. Add all four and a hotel ballroom stops looking like a hotel ballroom.
How the rig gets run depends on what is in it. DJ lighting is set up, aimed, tested and put into sound reactive mode or patched to your DJ's controller, so the fixtures follow the music all night and your DJ runs the looks. We deliver, place, aim, set the mode, and come back after the gig to strike. If you would rather have the looks run by hand, ask for a lighting engineer and we will put one on the job to run them live. For more involved lighting, moving heads and anything cued to a show, we recommend that engineer on a lighting console.
We build the rig around your floor either way. It is part of the wider event lighting we do, and it works whether we are your DJ or your DJ is somebody else entirely.

Moving Heads
## One moving head does the work of six fixed lights.
A moving head, the family of fixtures also called intelligent lighting, is a lamp mounted in a motorized yoke that pans, tilts, changes color, changes beam shape and dims on cue. A static fixture points at one thing all night. A moving head points at whatever the song needs at that moment, and then somewhere else eight bars later.
Practically, that is what buys the variety. The same four fixtures can sit still and wash the floor in warm amber during dinner, then open into fast sweeping beams over the crowd an hour later, then lock into a tight cone on a couple for a spotlight dance. You are renting fixtures that produce all six looks rather than six separate looks.
They come in broad families: wash heads with soft wide output for covering people and floor, and spot or beam heads with a tight hard edge for cutting through air and projecting patterns. Most rooms want some of each. Moving heads are where a lighting console comes in, and where a lighting engineer is worth adding on complex setups. They are patched and programmed by our crew, then run by your DJ or live by the engineer as part of the show.

The Layers
## What goes into a dance floor rig.
Not every event needs all of these, and part of our job is telling you which ones your room genuinely benefits from. This is the vocabulary, and knowing it makes every lighting conversation you have, with us or anyone else, a shorter one.
Layer One
### Moving head wash
Soft-edged, wide-output moving fixtures that put color onto the floor and the people on it. This is the layer that makes a dance floor feel like a defined place rather than a patch of carpet, and because the heads move, the same fixtures cover the cake table earlier in the night and the dance floor later.
Best for Every event. This is the foundation layer.
Layer Two
### Moving head spot & beam
Hard-edged, tight-output heads that throw a visible shaft of light instead of a soft pool. These are what produce the sweeping, crossing beams over a crowd, the aerial fans, and the sharp pattern work on floors and walls. They are also what most people are picturing when they say they want the room to look like a concert.
Best for Receptions after dinner, school dances, club nights, live bands, reveals.
Layer Three
### Static color wash & uplighting
Fixed LED fixtures around the perimeter and along the walls, holding a color that the moving lights work against. Uplighting is doing a different job from the dance floor rig. It dresses the room, and the two are designed together, because a room the venue keeps lit brightly is what dance floor lighting has to work against.
Best for Ballrooms, barns, tents, anywhere with walls worth using.
Layer Four
### Effect fixtures
Derby, wash-bar and multi-beam effect fixtures that fill air and floor with fast-moving color across a wide angle. They do the one thing moving heads leave to them: cover everything at once. Used well they sit underneath the rest of the rig and give it energy; used alone they are what makes a room read as under-lit rather than designed. These are the fixtures that run sound reactive by default, following the music on their own. At a recent wedding the uplights did the same trick: after the bride's surprise reveal in alternating pinks, we opened the floor and the whole perimeter followed the beat of the music for the rest of the party.
Best for Peak-of-the-night dancing, proms, quinceañeras, party sets.
Punctuation
### Strobe & blinder
High-output white fixtures used in seconds, not minutes, a drop, a chorus, a countdown, a grand exit. Strobes point at the floor and blinders point back at the crowd. Both are entirely about restraint: they land because they are rare, and we always check photosensitivity concerns and venue rules before programming them in.
Best for Club and rave nights, EDM sets, countdowns, high-energy receptions.
The Air
### Haze & atmospheric effects
A beam is invisible until there is something in the air for it to reflect off. A light, even haze is what turns moving heads from bright dots into visible shafts of light. It is a small addition to any rig and the one that makes the beams you are paying for visible. Venue clearance and alarm coordination are ours to handle.
Best for Any event with beam fixtures. Essentially mandatory for aerials.
Scale
### Lasers & specialty effects
Staffed laser systems with safety planning and audience-scanning discipline, for events big enough that the lighting rig alone will not carry the moment. A technician runs them live all night. There is a dedicated page on how we run them.
Best for Concerts, festivals, after-parties, EDM and club events, major reveals.
Structure
### Truss, totems & rigging
Fixtures need to be up in the air to do anything useful, and how they get there changes with every venue. Ground-supported truss, uprights and totem stands cover most rooms while leaving the building untouched, which is what churches, historic venues and most hotels require. Cable is routed and taped, and every guest path stays clear.
Best for Everywhere. This is the part nobody thinks about until load-in.
### Knowing which of these you want is our job
Most people arrive knowing what they want the room to feel like and not which fixtures produce it. That is the normal starting point. Send a photo of the room, a link to the venue, or a picture off Instagram of a dance floor you liked. That is more useful than a fixture list, and we will work backwards to the rig from there. Start at our quote form .
Designing To The Room
## What decides the size of the rig.
Two events on the same date with the same guest count can need completely different lighting. These are the six things we look at before proposing anything, and they are the reason every rig is quoted for its room.
### The dance floorThe floor is what we design for
A rig is designed to cover a specific piece of floor from specific angles. A 20×20 floor in the middle of a 300-person ballroom needs a completely different plot from a 40-foot-wide floor along one wall, even though the guest count is identical. Tell us the floor size and where it sits and half the design is already decided.
### Ceiling heightWhat the beams have room to do
High ceilings let fixtures get up where beams can spread and cross overhead; low ceilings mean shorter throws, flatter angles and different fixture choices to avoid blinding people at eye level. A room with a nine-foot ceiling is its own design, separate from a room with a twenty-foot one. It is a different problem.
### Rigging & positionsWhere fixtures can physically live
Some venues offer truss, catwalks or existing rigging points. Most have nowhere to hang from, in which case everything is ground-supported and needs floor space and clean sightlines. Historic and religious venues frequently prohibit attaching anything to the structure, which we plan around rather than argue with.
### PowerA common surprise
A real rig draws real power, and the circuit behind the DJ booth is often already carrying the audio. We confirm available circuits with the venue in advance and bring distribution and cable to reach them. Finding a power limit weeks out is a routine conversation, and finding it at load-in on a Saturday is a real problem.
### House lightsYour rig’s main competition
A lighting design lands when the ballroom comes down from full brightness. Part of the plan is agreeing in advance who dims what and when, venues vary from full dimming control to a single switch to lights that stay as they are. Where the house stays bright, we design for a bright house.
### The night itselfDinner and peak are different events
The same room needs warm, still, low-level light during dinner and something entirely different two hours later. A designed rig covers both from the same fixtures. Where you want that transition called by hand, running it is a big part of what a lighting engineer is there for. It also keeps the club lighting where it belongs, after dinner.

Questions
## DJ lighting rental, answered plainly.
What is a moving head light?
A moving head is a lighting fixture mounted in a motorized yoke, so it can pan, tilt, change color, change beam shape and dim on cue. It is the core of what the industry calls intelligent lighting. Because one fixture can produce many different looks over the course of a night, a handful of moving heads replaces a much larger number of static fixtures, and gives you variety a fixed rig cannot.
What is the difference between wash, spot and beam moving heads?
A wash head produces a soft, wide pool of light for covering people and floor in color. A spot head produces a hard-edged beam that can project patterns. A beam head produces a very tight, concentrated shaft designed to be seen in the air rather than land on a surface. Most well-designed dance floor rigs use a combination, because they solve different problems.
Can we rent DJ lighting without a DJ?
Yes. We light plenty of dance floors where the music is somebody else’s, another DJ, a band, or a venue’s in-house system. We design the rig, set it up and coordinate directly with whoever is running the show. If we are also your DJ, the lighting and the music share one crew and one cue sheet, which is the tighter version.
Does someone stay to run the lighting?
It depends on the rig. DJ lighting goes out in sound reactive mode or patched to your DJ's controller, so the fixtures follow the music and your DJ runs the looks. We deliver, place, aim, test it and come back after the event to strike. If you would rather the looks were run by hand, ask for a lighting engineer and we will put one on the job for the night. We recommend one for more involved lighting, moving heads and anything cued to a show, which runs from a lighting console.
Can we pick the lighting up and set it up ourselves?
Our crew handles that part. We deliver, rig, focus, test and strike everything ourselves, and a lighting engineer is available to run it live on the more complex rigs. That is partly about the result, fixtures aimed at the wrong angles produce none of the effect you are paying for, and partly about safety, since a dance floor rig puts heavy fixtures in the air and draws real power in a room full of people.
Do we need haze or fog?
If your rig includes beam fixtures, effectively yes. A beam of light is invisible until there is something in the air to reflect off it, so without haze you have paid for aerial effects nobody can see. Haze is a very light, even atmosphere that does not read as smoke. It does need venue clearance and sometimes fire-alarm coordination, and we handle both in advance.
Will the lighting work if our venue will not turn the house lights down?
It works, but differently, and we would rather plan for it than be surprised by it. Where the house cannot dim, we lean toward higher-output fixtures, stronger color on the walls and effects that read against ambient light, and we set expectations honestly. In most DFW venues some level of dimming is available, the key is agreeing in advance who controls it and when.
Do you have to attach anything to our venue?
Usually not. Most of our positions are ground-supported, truss, uprights and totem stands that touch nothing but the floor, which is what churches, historic venues and most hotels require. Where a venue has its own truss or rigging points and permits their use, we will use them. We confirm all of this with your venue before the day.
How much power does a dance floor rig need?
More than the single circuit behind a DJ booth, which is usually already carrying the audio. We confirm the available circuits with your venue in advance and bring distribution and cable to reach them. It is a routine conversation when it happens weeks out, and a real problem when it happens at load-in on a Saturday afternoon.
Can the lighting change between dinner and dancing?
That is one of the main reasons to use moving fixtures rather than static ones. The same rig holds a warm, still, low-level look through dinner and toasts, then opens into full color and movement when the floor does. A moving head rig runs from a lighting console, so we build looks for each part of your timeline, and your DJ or a lighting engineer on request runs the transitions. On a sound reactive rig, a lighting engineer is who calls that change by hand.
What areas of Dallas-Fort Worth do you cover?
The whole Metroplex, roughly a forty-mile radius from the mid-cities, covering Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, Frisco, Irving, Southlake, McKinney, Richardson, Grapevine, Denton and everywhere in between. If your venue is further out, ask anyway and we will tell you honestly whether it works.

Gobo projection
## Gobo, custom gobo monogram and full color laser projection
Gobo is the trade word for the same thing. Here is what it means and why the file we build looks so different from the proof you approve.
A gobo is the disc that sits in front of a light and cuts the beam into a shape. When a lighting company says custom gobo monogram, they mean what a bride means by wedding monogram: your design, put up as light. The difference between an old gobo and what we run is color. A cut metal gobo gives you one color, usually white. A laser projector reproduces a full color file, so the design on the left below is projected on the right with its gold rings and its watercolor florals intact.
Full color gold and floral wedding monogram design file.
The same monogram projected on a board and batten wall in daylight.
That second frame is also a daylight test, and we are showing it on purpose. The design on painted siding in the afternoon is soft and low in contrast. Outdoors a projected monogram needs full dark and a light-colored surface to land on, so an outdoor gobo projection is a post-sunset item on the timeline.
The pair below is the part clients ask about right after they approve a proof. What you sign off on is black artwork on a cream background, because that is how a design reads on a screen and on paper. The projection file is the inverse of it: white artwork on transparent. A projector adds light, so wherever your design is dark on the proof, the projection file has to be empty. We build both files, we show you both, and the thing on the wall matches the thing you approved.
Wedding monogram design proof in black on cream.
The same design inverted to white for projection.

FAQ
## Questions about monogram projector rental in Dallas-Fort Worth
What is a monogram projector?
A monogram projector is a lighting fixture that puts a custom design, usually your names and date or a company logo, onto a wall or a ceiling. The design lives in a file we build for you, and the projector shows it as light rather than as a printed sign.
Can the monogram be more than our initials?
Yes. We project names, dates, phrases, crests, full logos and artwork pulled from an invitation suite. Three lines of text plus a date is a normal design for us. If it can be drawn, it can be projected.
Will the monogram show up with the room lights on?
It will be visible, and it will be soft. The room light level is what decides how a projected monogram reads, more than the fixture does. If you want it crisp in photographs, plan on the monogram being at its strongest after dinner, when the venue brings the house lights down for dancing.
Which surface should the monogram go on?
A wall or a ceiling, every time. Those surfaces hold the whole design all night and stay clear in photographs, because the light lands on a flat plane above the crowd. Send us your floor plan and we will pick the wall that carries it best in your room.
Is the projection full color or one color?
Full color. The fixture uses a laser light source, so it reproduces a color file the way a screen does. Gold, blush, navy and watercolor florals all come through. A traditional cut metal gobo is limited to a single color, and that is the difference people notice.
How does the design process work?
You send us your names, your date and any artwork you already have. We build a proof and email it to you. Two rounds of changes are normal, and the timeline is comfortable as long as we have approved artwork about a week before the event.
Can you project our company logo instead of a wedding monogram?
Yes. Corporate logo projection is the same service with a different file. We project company logos, event slogans, sponsor marks and conference branding onto stage walls, lobby walls and ballroom walls.
Do you set the monogram projector up, or do we?
We set it up. A technician brings the projector, the stand or clamp and the cable, places the fixture where the beam is clean, focuses the design and tests it against the room light, and our crew picks it up after the event. A technician handles every part of it, from the proof to the focus.
What areas of Dallas-Fort Worth do you cover?
We cover roughly forty miles from ZIP 76053, which takes in Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Irving, Plano, Frisco, McKinney, Denton, Grapevine, Southlake and the venues in between. If your venue is further out, ask anyway and we will tell you honestly whether it works.

Common Questions
## Laser show questions, answered straight.
Do I need a permit for a laser light show?
Laser light shows require an FDA/CDRH variance to operate legally in the United States. We hold the variance and handle the compliance side as part of the booking, including the paperwork your venue may ask for.
Can laser light shows be used outdoors?
Yes. Our 40W systems are designed specifically for festivals and large outdoor venues. Outdoor shows add one step, airspace coordination, which we take care of ahead of your event date.
Is a laser light show safe for guests?
Yes, when operated by a trained technician with properly rated equipment, which is why we staff every laser rental with our own operator. Beam paths and audience scanning zones are planned before the event, not improvised during it.
What's the difference between 5W, 10W, and 40W lasers?
Power determines brightness, how far the beams stay visible, and how much space the show can cover. A 5W system is right for an indoor room of around 200 guests; 10W handles most receptions and galas up to roughly 1,000; 40W is for large venues and open-air productions where the beams have to travel.
What is included in a rental?
We deliver, set up, run, and strike everything ourselves. An on-site technician comes with every laser booking, both for safety and because the show is programmed and run live.

What A Follow Spot Is
## What is a follow spot, and where do you rent one?
A follow spot is a high-output, hard-edged spotlight on a yoke, operated by a person who keeps its beam on someone as they move. It is the light that isolates a bride at the top of a staircase, holds a singer through a solo, or picks an award winner out of a table of ten and walks them to the stage. What makes it a follow spot is the person aiming it in real time.
That is also the answer to the second half of the question. A follow spotlight arrives with a plan: it needs a position with a clean sightline, a stable platform or truss, power run to it, a beam and frame size set for your room, and someone standing behind it who knows when the cue is coming. We rent the whole thing as one job: fixture, position, rigging, power and operator.
Everything else on this page is really about that one distinction. See the rest of what we do on the lighting services page, or tell us your venue and we will tell you where the spot needs to live in it.

The Operator Is The Rental
## A follow spot is an operator first, and a fixture second.
The hard part of a follow spot is the person behind it. It is knowing to pick someone up two seconds before the doors open rather than two seconds after, sizing the iris down as they come closer so the beam stays on their shoulders instead of swallowing the head table, and easing out under the last note instead of snapping to black.
Those are learned reflexes, and they are why every follow spotlight we send out goes with an operator from our own crew. They walk the room with you or your planner, take the cue list off your timeline, and sit through the rehearsal if there is one. When the timeline slips, and it usually slips, there is a person on the spot adjusting to the night as it happens.
It also means one less thing on your run sheet. The person standing on a platform in the dark for four hours is ours, already briefed and already scheduled.

What It Is For
## The moments a follow spot exists to serve.
A follow spot picks one person out for one moment; room lighting is a different fixture doing a different job. It runs on a handful of cues: the ones people came to see, and the ones that end up in the video.
The Doors Open
### Grand entrances
A wedding party, a couple, a guest of honor or a CEO walking into a dark room. The spot picks them up at the door and travels with them to the floor, which does two things at once: it tells four hundred people where to look, and it lights the faces that every phone in the room is already pointed at. With it, the entrance happens in a pool of light and the whole room sees it.
Best for Weddings, quinceañeras, galas, award dinners, milestone birthdays.
Three Minutes That Matter
### First dances & spotlight dances
House lights down, everything else off, one beam on two people in the middle of a floor. Photographers and videographers shoot all three minutes of it, and it is also the moment that most needs its own light rather than the glow of a DJ booth and an exit sign. A follow spot separates the couple from the room and follows them if they move, which choreographed dances always do.
Best for First dances, father-daughter and mother-son dances, choreographed routines.
Recognition
### Award presentations
The classic use, and the one corporate clients ask for by name. The spot finds the recipient at their table, holds them while they stand, and walks them to the stage, so the applause has somewhere to go and the camera has someone to find. On a long awards program it is also what keeps the show moving, quietly.
Best for Awards nights, galas, banquets, sales kickoffs, honors and recognition programs.
Production
### Theater, dance & pageants
Productions where the spot is written into the script rather than added to it: musical numbers, competition routines, crownings, solos and curtain calls. These need a real operator on a real cue sheet, sometimes two spots working opposite sides of a stage, with frame and color changes called from the booth. This is the version of the job closest to theatrical practice, and we run it that way.
Best for Pageants, recitals, competitions, school and community theater, dance productions.
Stage
### Concerts, bands & live music
A wash lights a band; a follow spot lights a person. Vocal solos, a guitarist stepping forward, a front-of-stage moment beyond the fixed rig, the spot is what tells an audience where the song is happening. Paired with stage wash and a designed rig it turns a lit stage into a show.
Best for Live bands, concerts, festivals, tribute nights, album release parties and battle-of-the-bands.
The Podium
### Keynotes & general sessions
Conference general sessions increasingly put the speaker in front of the lectern rather than behind it, and a fixed front wash stays where it was aimed while the speaker walks. A spot keeps a presenter properly lit anywhere on the stage, which matters most when the session is being recorded or streamed. Keeping the presenter in the light is what makes that footage worth using again.
Best for Conferences, general sessions, town halls, product reveals, streamed and recorded events.
Worship
### Church & houses of worship
Christmas and Easter productions, dramas, youth events, choir and worship-team features. Sanctuaries are usually lit for a fixed platform alone, so anything staged outside that platform needs its own light. A spot from the back of the room covers the aisle, the floor and the balcony steps, and it goes in on its own platform, leaving the building untouched.
Best for Holiday productions, dramas, baptisms, youth nights, guest speakers.
School
### Schools, colleges & graduations
Homecoming courts, talent shows, dance team features, honors ceremonies and graduation walks in gymnasiums that were built for basketball and lit accordingly. The spot is usually the only lighting decision that changes the whole feel of the event, which is why it is often the one thing a school books.
Best for Homecoming, prom, talent shows, graduations, honors assemblies, college productions.
Nightlife
### Club nights & special reveals
Bottle service arrivals, artist introductions, a car or product coming out from behind drape, a countdown moment. A hard beam cutting through haze is a different tool from wash and effect lighting, and it is what makes a reveal read as an event rather than a curtain being pulled.
Best for Club and rave nights, artist intros, product reveals, launches, New Year countdowns.

Spotlight Rental, Sorted Out
## “Spotlight rental” means four different things. Here is which one you want.
People arrive on this page asking for a spotlight and mean any one of these. They are genuinely different fixtures doing genuinely different jobs, and naming the right one is how an event ends up with lighting that does what was pictured.
### Follow spotMoves with a person
Rig 1 follow spot on a yoke · iris and frame · operator on it all night
A large, high-output spotlight on a yoke with an operator behind it, an iris to size the beam and a frame to shape it. It is the only one of these four that tracks somebody as they move. If the picture in your head involves a beam following a person across a floor, this is the one, and it is what the rest of this page is about.
### Pin spotAimed at an object, and it stays there
Rig 1 pin spot per object · focused at load-in · set and left
A small fixture throwing a tight beam at one fixed thing, a centerpiece, the cake, the head table, a display case. It is set at load-in and holds that position for the night, hands free. People often say “spotlight the cake” when what they want is a pin spot, which is a much smaller undertaking. We cover pin spots as part of a lighting design .
### Stage or ceremony washCovers a whole area at once
Rig 4 to 8 LED wash fixtures · stands or truss · set once
Front light across a defined space so faces read properly for the room, for photography and on camera. A wash exists to keep faces readable from the back of the room, and it stays quiet on purpose. Many events that ask for a follow spot need a wash first and a spot second, and we will say so.
### Moving head spotAutomated, and it runs to a timeline
Rig 2 or more moving heads · DMX console · programmed cues
A motorized intelligent fixture that pans, tilts and changes color on a programmed cue. It can hit a mark beautifully and it can sweep a room, but it is following a timeline rather than a person, and a follow spot has an operator who waits when a bride stops to hug her grandmother halfway down the aisle. Great for looks and reveals. An operated spot is the one that moves with a person.
### Not sure which one your moment needs?
Describe what you are picturing, who is moving, where they are going and how dark the room is, and we will tell you which fixture does it. Sometimes the honest answer is a pin spot and a wash rather than a follow spot, and that is a smaller conversation than the one you thought you were having. Start at our quote form .
Venue By Venue
## Where the spot goes in a room like yours.
Position is decided before anything else, because it determines the angle on faces, whether the beam clears the crowd, and what it lands on when it misses. This is the conversation we would have on a site visit.
### Hotel ballroomLow ceiling, floor-supported position
Position rear platform · flat throw · power run to the deck
The room we work in most often, and the one with the tightest constraints. Ceilings are often too low for a steep angle, so the spot goes on a platform at the back of the room and works at a flatter throw. That is workable, and it means the beam has to clear standing guests and a stack of centerpieces. We work that out in advance from your floor plan.
### Theater & auditoriumPurpose-built positions
Position house booth, catwalk or balcony rail · existing power
The easiest venues to work in, because someone already solved this: a booth, a catwalk or a balcony rail with power and sightlines. Our job here is mostly matching the house rig, working with the resident technician, and running cues to a stage manager’s calls rather than a wedding timeline.
### Church & sanctuaryFixed lighting, protected surfaces
Position freestanding rear platform or balcony · floor-standing power
Sanctuaries usually light one platform alone, and most limit what may be attached to the building. We work from a freestanding position at the back or from an existing balcony, cover the aisle and the floor as well as the platform, and leave the structure untouched. Coordinating with the facilities team early settles most of it.
### Gymnasium & multipurpose roomHeight, and a ground-supported position
Position ground-supported tower · platform · long power run
Plenty of ceiling, rigging that stays untouched, and overhead lighting that is either full-on or off. Ground-supported positions and a proper platform do the work. The gain is dramatic here because the baseline is so flat. One operated beam changes how a gym reads more than anything else you could bring into it.
### Barn, ranch & historic venueStructure, sightlines and rules
Position loft, truss or ground support · surveyed on site
Exposed trusses and lofts sometimes give a genuinely excellent position, and sometimes give an obstructed one. Historic venues add rules about what can be placed where. We look at the actual room before committing to a position, because the position is what decides whether the beam lands on the person or on the wall behind them.
### Tent & outdoorPower, weather and open sides
Position tower or scaffold platform · generator or venue power
Outdoors there is rarely power where the spot needs to be and rarely a structure to put it on, so the plan starts with a tower or platform and a power run. Wind, dew and temperature all get factored in. It is very doable. It is just a conversation that has to happen well before the week of.

Questions
## Follow spot rental, answered plainly.
What is a follow spot?
A follow spot is a high-output, hard-edged spotlight on a yoke that an operator aims by hand, keeping the beam on a person as they move. It has an iris to size the beam and a frame to shape it, and it is the only lighting fixture that genuinely tracks somebody in real time. That is what separates it from a pin spot, a wash or a programmed moving head.
Does the follow spot come with an operator?
Always, and it is not an optional extra. Every follow spot we send out goes with a trained operator from our own crew who works from your cue list, attends the rehearsal where there is one, and adapts live when the timeline moves. The fixture is the easy part. The operator is what you are renting.
Can we pick one up and run it ourselves?
No. A trained operator comes with every follow spot and stays on it. The practical parts (the position, the platform, the power run and the focus) all have to be right, an operated spot is a skill, and a missed pickup on a grand entrance is not a mistake you can fix afterwards.
Where does the follow spot go in the room?
Usually at the back, raised on a platform or ground support so the beam clears a room full of standing guests. Theaters and auditoriums often have a purpose-built booth, catwalk or balcony rail we can use instead. We work the position out from your venue in advance, because it decides the angle on faces and whether the sightline survives a full room.
What is the difference between a follow spot and a pin spot?
A follow spot is large, operated and moves with a person. A pin spot is small, fixed at load-in and aimed at one object, a centerpiece, a cake, a head table. People often say “spotlight the cake” when they mean a pin spot, which is a much smaller undertaking. Tell us what you are picturing and we will tell you which one it is.
Do you need to rig anything to our venue?
Usually not. Most of our positions are freestanding (a platform or ground support that touches nothing but the floor), which is what churches, historic venues and hotels generally require. Where a venue has its own catwalk or balcony position, we will use it. We confirm all of this with your venue before the day.
Do we need one spot or two?
One covers most weddings, awards nights and corporate sessions. Two are worth it when a stage is wide enough that a single side angle would leave someone half-lit, when two people need to be picked up independently, or when a production calls for opposite-side coverage (pageants, dance competitions and theatrical shows most often). We will tell you which yours is.
How do you know when the cues are?
We build a cue list off your timeline or run sheet and agree who is calling the show, whether that is your planner, your DJ, a stage manager or our own audio position. Our operator is on comms with them, has a printed cue sheet at the position, and attends the rehearsal or soundcheck where there is one. Timelines always move, and a person on the spot can move with them.
Can we add a follow spot to lighting or sound we have already booked?
Yes, and plenty of clients do. If you already have a DJ, a band or in-house AV, we supply the spot and the operator and coordinate directly with whoever is calling the show. If we are already handling your audio or lighting design, it shares a load-in, a crew and one cue sheet, which is the version where the light and the music land together.
What areas of Dallas-Fort Worth do you cover?
The whole Metroplex, roughly a forty-mile radius from the mid-cities, covering Dallas, Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano, Frisco, Irving, Southlake, McKinney, Richardson, Grapevine, Denton and everywhere in between. If your venue is further out, ask anyway and we will tell you honestly whether it works.

Fog And Haze Machine Rental
## Which fog machine do you need: haze, high density fog or low-lying fog?
Fog covers three separate machines. A hazer makes your lighting beams visible, a high output fogger fills a room on a drop, and a low-lying machine lays a cloud across the dance floor. Getting that choice right is most of what this page is for, so here is the difference in plain terms.
Haze
### Haze: beams you can see
Machine Chauvet Hurricane Haze 2D or 4D · water based · DMX
Haze is a thin, even suspension that makes light visible. On its own you barely notice it. The moment a moving head, a gobo wash, a pin spot on the cake table or a laser fires through it, every beam reads as a solid shaft of light. Haze is what makes a lighting package photograph the way it looked in the proposal, and guests read it as atmosphere rather than smoke.
Best for Ballrooms, chapels, corporate general sessions, and any room where lasers or moving heads are in the rig.
High density fog
### High density fog: a moment on a cue
Machine Froggy’s Fog Titan 1200 · 1,300 W · variable output
High density fog works the other way around. It is a heavy, opaque burst you use as a single moment: a grand entrance, a DJ drop, a first look, a Halloween walk through, or a photo and video setup that needs the background gone. It rolls in thick, does its job and clears.
Best for Grand entrances, club nights, Halloween events, concert sets and camera work.
Low-lying fog
### Low-lying fog: a cloud on the floor
Machine Chauvet DJ Cumulus or ADJ Entour Ice · dry ice or water based
Low-lying fog stays on the floor. It is the dancing on the clouds look, a knee deep cloud that hangs across the dance floor for a first dance or a quinceañera waltz, with the couple standing above it. That machine has a page of its own, and this page carries the rest of the fog and haze inventory.
Best for First dances, quinceañera waltzes, theatrical reveals and anything photographed close to the ground.

Machine Titan 1200 · 1,300 W · five-liter reservoir · variable 0 to 100 percent

Low-Lying Fog And Dry Ice
## Low-lying fog and dry ice: dancing on the clouds.
Low-lying fog is a cloud that stays on the floor instead of rising, and two machines produce it. The Chauvet DJ Cumulus makes the effect on water alone, using an onboard ultrasonic agitator to turn distilled water into a fine mist that chills the fog so it hugs the floor. The ADJ Entour Ice is the theatrical version, dropping dry ice into heated water the way stage productions have done it for decades, built as a wheeled, insulated, DMX controllable machine.
Dry ice fog reads denser, whiter and colder than the water based version, and it hugs the floor harder, which is why it is still the standard for a first dance, a quinceañera waltz or a theatrical reveal photographed close to the ground. Dry ice has to be sourced fresh on the day and handled safely, and that part is ours.
Because low-lying fog is a whole package rather than a single machine, the full detail has its own page: coverage, how long a cloud holds, what the dry ice service includes, and how it is timed against the song.

The effect, by the name most people use
## Dancing on the clouds
Dancing on the clouds is a knee-deep layer of white fog laid flat across the dance floor. It stays down at floor level, leaves the air above it clear, and holds its edge at the tables. The couple stands above it rather than inside it, which is the whole point: from the front row and from the photographer’s position, the floor disappears and the two of you appear to be standing on a cloud.
It works because the fog is chilled. Warm fog rises and fills a room; cold fog sinks and stays. All four of our sizes do that same job by a slightly different route, three chill the fog by passing it through a basket of dry ice, and the fourth chills it with an onboard ultrasonic water system and runs on fluid alone.
People search for this effect under half a dozen names, dancing on the clouds, a cloud machine, low lying fog, ground fog, dry ice fog, a low fog machine for a first dance. They are all the same look. What differs is which machine gets used, how long the cloud holds, and whether anyone is standing there running it.
A dry ice cloud lasts as long as the dry ice load lasts. The size of the ice basket is what sets that.
The one thing nobody tells you before you book
The part that decides everything
## How long the cloud lasts
This is the question that matters and it is the one most rental listings leave out. A dry ice cloud machine works by dropping a basket of dry ice into heated water. Fog is produced for as long as there is ice in the basket. When the ice is gone, the cloud stops, and it stops all at once. So the honest answer to “how long does it last” is a number that belongs to your booking rather than to the machine: however long the ice load in that particular machine lasts, at the output level it is being run at.
Which means the size of the ice basket is the specification that governs your event. A machine with a small basket can carry one song beautifully. A machine with a large basket can carry a grand entrance walk, hold through the introductions, and still have ice left for the first dance. Running a small machine hard to cover a long moment is how people end up with a cloud that dies halfway through the chorus.
So it is easier to think of what we own as four sizes of the same effect rather than four machines, a ladder from one defining moment up to all night long. One of them comes to your event. These are the four rungs, smallest load to largest.
### Nimbus JuniorSize 01 · 8 lb dry ice
One defining moment. Intimate floors, small chapels, tight reception rooms where a large machine has nowhere to sit.
### NimbusSize 02 · 12 lb dry ice
The workhorse, and what most weddings book. Longer hold, and enough in the basket to cover back-to-back dances rather than one.
### ADJ Entour IceSize 03 · 30 lb dry ice · DMX
The largest load we carry, and the one that fires on a lighting cue from the console instead of by hand. Ballrooms, long entrance walks, corporate reveals.
### Chauvet CumulusSize 04 · continuous
Runs on distilled water and fluid, refillable while it is running. It runs on fluid rather than an ice load, so it holds for as long as you want it.
The second half of the answer is timing. Dry ice machines need to come up to temperature before they produce, and the ice has to go in close to the moment, because it starts sublimating the second it hits the water. So we agree the running order with your planner and your DJ or band in advance, and our technician loads and fires on the cue. The cloud peaks on the beat the song starts on. That is a coordination job as much as an equipment one, and it is why someone stands with the machine instead of leaving it switched on in a corner.
When a moment is genuinely too long for one load, or the floor is genuinely too wide for one machine, we bring two. Machines can be combined for back-to-back effects, one covering the grand entrance and a second held in reserve for the first dance, or run side by side to cover a larger floor evenly instead of pushing one unit past what it can do.
Low lying fog, running
The layer sits at knee height and stays there. That is the entire trick, and it is a question of temperature rather than of how much fog the machine can make.

Size 01 · 8 lb load
### Nimbus Junior

Questions we get every week
## Dry ice and low lying fog, answered
How long does a dancing on the clouds effect last?
For as long as the dry ice load lasts, and no longer. A dry ice machine makes fog by dropping ice into heated water, so output continues while there is ice in the basket and stops when there is not. That is why basket size is the specification that matters, and why we own the effect in four sizes rather than one machine: the 8 lb size is built for one defining moment, the 12 lb size covers back-to-back dances, and the 30 lb size carries a long entrance and still has ice left. The fourth size runs on fluid rather than dry ice, so it holds for as long as you want it. Rather than quote you a number that depends entirely on how hard the machine is run, we ask what moments you want covered and bring the machine that covers them.
What is the difference between dry ice fog and a regular fog machine?
Temperature, and therefore where the fog goes. A standard fog or haze machine produces warm fog, which rises and fills the room, useful for making light beams visible, useless for a cloud effect. Dry ice fog is chilled, so it sinks and stays flat at ankle-to-knee height, holds a defined edge, and dissipates without hazing the room or drifting over the tables. If you want the floor to disappear, you need the cold kind. If you want the air to glow around a lighting rig, you want the warm kind, and those are two different machines.
Do you deliver, set up and run the machine, or is this a pickup rental?
We deliver, set up and run it. A technician brings the machine, positions it for the room, sources and loads the dry ice, takes the cue from your DJ or bandleader, operates the effect and packs it down afterwards. Everything from the ice to the strike is on us. Most low lying fog listings in Dallas-Fort Worth are twenty-four-hour box rentals with the ice and the setup left to you; that is a genuinely different product, and it is worth checking which one you are comparing us against.
Do I need to buy the dry ice?
We handle it. We source it, transport it and load it, and we bring the right quantity for the machine and for the number of moments you want covered. Dry ice needs the right supplier, the right quantity, safe handling and correct timing, and it sublimates away whether you are using it or not, so ordering it the morning of your wedding is a job worth keeping off your own list. Handling all of that is part of the booking.
Is low lying fog safe for guests, the dance floor and the photographer?
It is a widely used effect and we run it with a technician present for that reason. The fog is water vapor chilled by carbon dioxide, it stays low, and it clears on its own. Our technician places the machine so the output lays flat across the floor rather than pooling at one edge, keeps the floor in view for the whole effect, and manages output if the room is behaving differently than expected. Floors can become slightly damp with heavy use, so we place and run it with that in mind, and we will always talk through anything specific to your venue or your guests beforehand.
Will the fog set off the venue's smoke detectors?
We will not tell you it cannot happen, because any airborne effect can interact with a detector. What we do is clear the effect with the venue in advance and, where the venue uses one, with their alarm monitoring company, and then place the machines away from detectors and return air vents. Many venues have a defined process for fog effects and need advance notice; some restrict dry ice entirely, which is one of the reasons we own a machine that does not use it. Tell us the venue early and we will handle that conversation before the date rather than on it.
Can we use the cloud effect for the grand entrance and the first dance?
Yes, and this is the situation that decides which machine we bring. Two separated moments need either one large load or two machines. We can combine machines for back-to-back effects, with one covering the grand entrance and a second held in reserve for the first dance, or run two side by side to cover a larger floor evenly rather than pushing a single unit past what it can do. Tell us every moment you want the cloud on and we will build the plan around all of them instead of hoping one load stretches.
Do you rent low lying fog machines outside of weddings?
Regularly. Quinceanera waltzes, milestone birthdays, corporate grand entrances and product reveals, photo shoots and video shoots. The corporate reveals usually run on our DMX machine so the effect fires inside a programmed lighting cue, and shoots usually run on the continuous machine because a camera crew resets more often than a dry ice load allows. Same fleet, same technician, same approach. We ask what the moment is and bring the machine that fits it.

Permits, Pyrotechnicians And The Fire Marshal
## Read this part first. It decides whether you can have sparks at all.
We put this at the top of the page so the venue's questions two weeks before the wedding already have answers. Here is the whole requirement, up front, in the order it happens.
### Cold sparks are a permitted effect in Dallas-Fort Worth.
A cold spark machine produces a fountain of sparkles at a far lower temperature than traditional pyrotechnics, which is why venues will consider it indoors and near people at all. It is still a regulated effect, and it still requires a permit. Every jurisdiction in the Metroplex has its own fire department and its own fire marshal, so the answer for a ballroom in Dallas is its own answer, separate from the same effect in Fort Worth, Arlington, Plano or Frisco. We handle the process either way; you just have to give us the runway to do it.
01
A licensed pyrotechnician operates the effect
A licensed pyrotechnician sets the machines, positions them, and fires them. That job belongs to the operator alone, whatever else the DJ, the venue or your own team is handling that night. It is a legal requirement rather than a service upgrade, and it is a common reason a cheaper quote from somewhere else falls apart at the venue walkthrough.
02
A permit from the fire department with jurisdiction
The effect has to be permitted by the fire department covering your venue’s address. We prepare and file the application with the equipment details, the operator’s credentials and the certificate of insurance. Approval is the authority’s decision, and we tell you a permit is in hand only once it is issued.
03
Four to six weeks of lead time
Permits take four to six weeks. That window is working time. It covers filing, the review, any questions that come back, and a re-submission if something on the plan has to move. Booking earlier is always better. Booking inside that window means we may not be able to run the effect, and we would rather tell you that now than the week of your event.
04
A floor plan approved by the fire marshal and the venue
The fire marshal has to approve a floor plan together with your venue, where each machine sits, how far it stands from guests, from décor and from anything overhead, and how the exits and egress routes stay clear. Your venue has to be on board before the plan goes in, so the earliest useful step you can take is asking them whether they allow cold sparks at all.
The short version: ask your venue first, then talk to us at least four to six weeks out. Everything after that is our job, the application, the operator, the insurance certificate, the floor plan and the crew on the night.

How Cold Spark Machines Work
## What a cold spark machine is.
It helps to know what you are permitting. Cold spark machines are their own category: a cold, contained plume, closer to a stage effect than to pyrotechnics. They are their own thing, which is why the rules around them are their own thing too.
### A fountain of sparkles, cool enough to touchWhat it produces
The machine heats a granular metallic composition and ejects it upward as a plume of bright sparkles that arc out and burn away in the air. What the room sees is a fountain of white-gold sparks rising several feet and falling as glitter. The effect is cold, the air stays clear, and the plume burns out in the air.
### Much cooler than pyrotechnicsWhy venues consider it indoors
The effect runs at a fraction of the temperature of a traditional pyrotechnic gerb, which is the whole reason it can be used close to a dance floor, under a normal ceiling height, and near people in formalwear. That is what earns it a conversation with a venue, and it is still a permitted effect, which is the part the fire marshal will confirm.
### Height is set, not guessedSpark fountain rental
Machines are configured for the height the room and the approved plan allow, so a low-ceilinged historic venue gets a different effect from a hotel ballroom with a thirty-foot ceiling. The height, the duration and the placement are all part of what goes on the floor plan, which means the effect you see on the night is the effect that was approved.
### Fired on a cue, not on a guessTiming
Our operator runs the machines against the actual cue, the downbeat of the first dance, the doors opening, the moment the award is announced. When we are also running your sound and lighting, that cue is shared across the whole rig, so the sparks, the music and the lighting hit as one thing instead of three near-misses.
### Two machines, four machines, a line of themQuantity
Most events use a pair flanking a dance floor or a doorway. Bigger rooms and stage reveals use four or more in a line, which reads as a wall of sparks rather than two points of light. The approved floor plan and the room decide how many you can use, so we settle that with the venue before the application goes in.
### Indoors and outdoorsIndoor sparklers
Indoors is where cold sparks matter most, because it is the setting where cold sparks are the one spark effect a venue can say yes to. Outdoors works too, with the usual caveats about wind and about where the plume lands. Either way the placement is fixed on the approved plan rather than decided on the day.
### What people usually put around it
Sparks are a punctuation mark, so they land hardest when the rest of the moment is built too. The usual additions are low-lying fog for a first dance, lasers and event lighting for the reveal, and CO2 effects, which live on the special effects page. If there is a speech or an announcement anywhere near the moment, the microphones we send out carry our AI-powered De-Feedback system as standard, so the introduction arrives clean.

Questions
## What people ask before booking cold sparks.
Do you rent cold spark machines in Dallas?
Yes. We supply and operate cold spark machines across Dallas, Fort Worth and the surrounding DFW area for weddings, corporate events, clubs and private parties. It is not a drop-off rental, the effect is delivered, placed to an approved floor plan and fired by a licensed pyrotechnician, because that is what the permit requires.
Do cold sparks need a permit?
Yes. Cold sparks are a permitted effect, and the permit comes from the fire department with jurisdiction over your venue’s address. The application has to be filed in advance, the operator has to be a licensed pyrotechnician, and the floor plan showing machine placement and clearances has to be approved by the fire marshal together with the venue. We prepare and file all of it; the approval itself is the authority’s decision.
How far in advance do I need to book cold sparks?
Four to six weeks at minimum, because that is how long permits take. That window covers filing, review, any questions that come back from the fire marshal, and a re-submission if something on the floor plan has to move. Earlier is always better. If your date falls inside that window, tell us anyway and we will give you a straight answer about whether it can still be done.
Can cold sparks be used indoors?
That is the setting they were made for. A cold spark machine runs at a far lower temperature than traditional pyrotechnics, which is why venues will consider it indoors near a dance floor when handheld sparklers and conventional pyro are not options at all. It still needs the permit and the approved floor plan, and your venue has to allow it, asking them is the first thing worth doing.
Are cold sparks safe?
They are designed to be used close to people, which is why the requirements exist. The effect is cold and the plume burns out in the air, and the machines are set to distances from guests, décor and anything overhead that the fire marshal has approved in advance. The safety comes from the approved plan and the licensed operator as much as from the machine.
Can I set up the cold spark machines myself?
No. Every cold spark rental goes out with our crew, and on a permitted effect that is the law rather than a preference, the permit is issued on the basis that a licensed pyrotechnician operates it. Everything is delivered, placed, fired and removed by our crew.
How many cold spark machines do I need?
Most events use a pair flanking a dance floor or a doorway. Larger rooms and stage reveals use four or more in a line, which reads as a wall of sparks rather than two points of light. The number is settled by the room and the approved floor plan rather than by an order form, so we work it out with your venue before the application goes in.
Can I use cold sparklers for a wedding entrance or first dance?
Those are the two most requested moments, along with the last song of the night. A pair of machines at the edge of the dance floor fired on the chorus is the shot that tends to end up framed. Because an operator fires it on the cue rather than a crowd lighting sparklers at once, it happens right when the music says it should.
Can I add fog, lasers or CO2 to the same booking?
Yes, and most people do, because the moment lands harder when it is built rather than bolted on. Low-lying fog under a first dance, lasers and lighting on a reveal, and CO2 effects all come from the same warehouse and the same load-in. Fog is on the dancing on the clouds page and the rest is on the special effects page.
How much does a cold spark machine rental cost in Dallas?
We do not publish prices, because a two-machine first dance and a stage reveal in a permitted arena are different jobs and one number would misprice both. ## Which special effect suits the moment you are planning?
Most people arrive here with a picture in their head and a name they are still looking for. The white blast over a dance floor, the silver fountains behind a couple, the beams cutting across a ballroom and the cloud that sits on the ground are four separate machines with four separate rigs. ### CO2 cannons and guns: a white plume
Rig 2 handheld CO2 guns · 2 CO2 cannons with LEDs on DMX · CO2 supplied
A burst of liquid CO2 leaves the nozzle and flashes into a column of white vapor that shoots overhead and vanishes in a few seconds. It is cold rather than hot, it leaves the floor dry, and it lands on a beat. This is the one effect that lives on this page alone, so it gets the long version further down.
Best for Club nights, DJ drops, raves, birthday entrances and hype moments in a corporate general session.
Cold sparks
### Cold sparks: silver fountains
Rig Cold spark machines · licensed pyrotechnician · permit, book 4 to 6 weeks out
Cold spark machines throw a fountain of silver sparks several feet into the air from a granule that burns far cooler than traditional pyrotechnics. Guests read it as fireworks indoors. It is the effect people mean when they say sparklers for the first dance. It is also the one effect here that has to be permitted and run by a licensed pyrotechnician, so it needs the longest lead time of anything on this page.
Best for First dances, grand entrances, cake cuttings, quinceañera waltzes and stage reveals.

Rig Laser projectors · run with haze · aimed above head height

Rig Hazers for beams · high density foggers for a burst
Haze is a thin, even suspension that makes every beam in the room read as a solid shaft of light. High density fog is the opposite job: a heavy burst behind a doorway for a silhouette entrance, gone within a minute. Both machines are covered in full on their own page.

CO2 Cannon And CO2 Gun Rental
## CO2 cannons and CO2 guns: a white plume on the drop.
Rig 2 handheld CO2 guns for your hands · 2 CO2 cannons with LEDs on DMX, technician run · CO2 supplied
Our CO2 guns and cannons create plumes of cold white smoke that shoot overhead and clear in seconds. Liquid CO2 travels from a tank through a hose to the nozzle, and the pressure drop at the nozzle flashes it into vapor and ice crystals. That is what you see: a bright white column that reads as an explosion on camera and disappears before the next bar of the song.
We carry two of each shape, and they are used in two different ways. The two handheld CO2 guns go in your hands. We charge them, show you the trigger and stand close by, then the couple, the guest of honor or whoever you want holding them fires the plume where they want it, straight up over the dance floor or out across the crowd. Most of the best photographs we get all year come from that thirty seconds. The two mounted cannons are ours to run. They have LED lights in the head and sit on DMX with the rest of the lighting rig, so the plume comes out lit in a color, and a technician fires them from the board on cues the DJ calls and the timeline sets. That is what puts the blast on the drop, on the entrance or on the reveal instead of a second behind it.
The reason CO2 gets used indoors so freely is that the plume is cold and it leaves the room clean. The plume is cold, the floor stays dry and the room is clear afterwards, so it suits venues that hold a firm line on flame and residue. What it does need is height above the nozzle and a clear path for the plume, which we check when we walk the room.
We bring the CO2, set the tanks, run the hose so it stays out of the walkway, and stay with the rig for the length of the event. The cannons fire from our board on DMX, cued off the DJ and the run of show. The handhelds are yours for the moment you want them, with our technician on them either side of the hit, loading, checking pressure and taking them back afterwards. When we are running your audio and lighting as well, the cannon cue is shared across the room, so the blast, the light and the drop land as one thing.

## Cold sparks: indoor sparkle fountains for the moment everyone films.
Cold spark machines create cascades of silver sparks that rise several feet and fall away, and they do it at a temperature low enough that many venues allow them where real pyrotechnics are refused. Guests read the effect as fireworks indoors. Photographers love it because the sparks light faces from below while the couple stays in focus.
These are the machines people are describing when they ask about sparklers for a first dance, cold sparklers for a wedding, or spark fountains for a stage entrance. Placement, the safe distance to the nearest guest and clearance overhead all get agreed with your venue before the date instead of worked out on the night.

Fog And Haze Machine Rental
## Fog and haze: the air that makes every other effect visible.
Haze is a thin suspension you barely notice until a beam passes through it, and then every moving head, pin spot and laser in the room reads as a shaft of light. High density fog does the opposite job. It is a heavy white burst you use as one moment, usually behind a doorway for a grand entrance, and it clears within a minute.
Because haze is what lets lasers and beam fixtures exist in the air, it gets added to most effects packages by default. Machine choice, venue rules and the difference between fog, haze and smoke are all set out on our fog machine and haze rental page . We deliver, place and test the machine, your DJ, your planner or you turn it on when it's time, and we pick it up after the event.

Dancing On The Clouds
## Dancing on the clouds: low-lying fog for a first dance.
Low-lying fog is chilled so it hangs at ankle height across the dance floor instead of rising, which gives you the dancing on the clouds look: a couple standing on a white cloud with faces clear above it. Dry ice produces the denser, whiter version and has been the theatrical standard for decades; a water based machine gives you a continuous cloud on fluid alone.
How much floor a cloud covers, how long it holds and how it is timed against the song matter more here than the machine does, which is why the clouds effect keeps a page to itself.
### The full clouds service
Coverage, dry ice handling and timing are covered on our dancing on the clouds page . Weddings book this alongside cold sparks often: a cloud under the first dance, then sparks as the song lands.

What We Clear Before The Date
## Every venue has rules about effects, and we settle them in advance.
Special effects are the part of an event most likely to run into a house rule, and finding that out on the day is expensive. So before your date we take the venue name, contact the room, and agree what is allowed, where the rig sits and what paperwork they want. Most rooms in the Metroplex we have worked before, so the answer usually comes back the same week.
### Detectors and alarm monitoring
Fog and haze can trigger smoke detectors, so we clear the effect with the venue and with the alarm monitoring company where there is one, and place machines away from detectors and return vents.
### Ceiling height and clearance
CO2 plumes and spark fountains both need room above the nozzle. We measure the height over the exact spot the effect fires from, because that is the number that governs the plume.
### Floor plan and safe distance
Where guests stand, where the cake table sits and how far the nearest chair is all shape the placement. That plan goes to the venue before load in.
### Overhead rigging and drapery
Drape, greenery, chandeliers and low truss all change what an effect can do underneath them. We look up during the walk through, not during the reception.
### Permits, licensing and insurance
Cold sparks are permitted and fired by a licensed pyrotechnician, and permit approval runs four to six weeks. Every rental carries full insurance, with a certificate for your venue whenever they ask for one, supplied ahead of load in.
### Power and cable paths
Effects share circuits with audio and lighting, so we plan the power draw and run hose and cable clear of every guest path.

Questions
## Special effects rental questions.
What special effects do you rent in Dallas-Fort Worth?
CO2 cannons and handheld CO2 guns, cold spark machines, laser light shows, fog and haze machines, and low-lying fog for the dancing on the clouds effect. Every one of these extras is delivered, rigged, cleared with your venue and tested by our crew, then loaded out afterward. How do CO2 cannons work at an event?
Liquid CO2 runs from a tank through a hose to the nozzle. The pressure drop at the nozzle flashes the liquid into vapor and ice crystals, which is the white plume you see shooting overhead. It rises, spreads and disappears within a few seconds, so it works as a hit on a beat instead of continuous atmosphere. Our two mounted cannons carry LED lights in the head and run on DMX, so the plume can come out lit in a color that matches the lighting cue.
Are CO2 cannons safe to use indoors?
CO2 is a cold effect that leaves the floor dry and the carpet clean, and venues that refuse open flame will frequently still allow it. What it needs is height above the nozzle and a clear path for the plume, plus a ventilated room. We check both when we walk your venue and we agree the placement with the room before your date.
What is the difference between cold sparks and CO2?
Cold sparks throw a silver fountain upward from a granule and read as fireworks indoors, which suits a first dance or a cake cutting. CO2 creates a white column of cold vapor that vanishes in seconds, which suits a drop, a reveal or a club room. Sparks are the romantic effect and CO2 is the hype effect, and plenty of events run both at different points in the night.
Will fog or haze set off the smoke detectors at my venue?
It can, which is why we settle it before your date. Manufacturers state plainly that atmospheric effects can trigger detectors, so we clear the effect with your venue and with the alarm monitoring company where there is one, then place machines so the output stays away from detectors and return vents. Some rooms allow haze but restrict heavy fog, and we will tell you which yours is.

Delivery, placement, testing and collection come with every effects booking. Fog and haze get switched on by you, your DJ or your planner when it's time. The cannons, the lasers, the sparks and the clouds stay on our board, cued off the DJ and the timeline.
Can I book more than one effect for the same event?
Yes, and most events do. A wedding might take a low-lying cloud for the first dance and cold sparks as the song lands, while a club night takes haze all evening with CO2 on the drops. Booking them together means one crew, one load in and one contract, and the cues get programmed against each other rather than fired by different people guessing.
How far in advance should I book special effects?
For CO2, lasers, fog, haze and clouds, two to four weeks is comfortable, mostly so there is time to clear the effect with your venue before the date, and shorter notice is often workable in a room we already know. Cold sparks are the exception and need longer: the permit takes four to six weeks to approve, so book those as soon as you have a date. Send us the date and the venue name and you will get a straight answer back.

## Projector and screen rental, matched as one package
Most people searching for a projector rental in Dallas need a screen with it, and the two have to agree with each other. A bright projector needs the right screen surface, and a beautiful screen needs a projector with the lumens to feed it; the image on the wall comes from the pair. So we rent them as a set. You tell us the room and the audience size, and the projector and screen come out of our inventory already paired for that job.
Every setup goes out the same way. Our crew delivers it, rigs the screen, dresses the cable, connects your laptop, tunes the image for the light in the room, and stays long enough to confirm your first slide looks right on the screen. Then we come back and pick it all up. We carry it in, set it up and carry it back out.

## Ultra short throw projector rental and ambient light rejecting screens for bright rooms
Rig Epson PowerLite 700U · 150 inch CLR screen · ultra short throw
This is the setup for a room that stays lit. The Epson PowerLite 700U is a 4,000 lumen WUXGA laser projector that sits inches from the screen instead of across the room, and it is paired with an Elite Screens Light-On CLR StarBright ambient light rejecting screen at 150 inches. The screen surface is built to reject the light coming down from the ceiling and accept only the light coming up from the projector, so the image holds its contrast with the house lights on.
Because the throw distance is inches rather than feet, the beam clears the room, so your slide stays clean and the middle of the room stays open for seating. Lobbies, hotel prefunction space, retail activations, reception areas and glass-walled conference rooms are all rooms we bring this setup to. Clients stop asking us whether they can dim the lights, because the image holds either way. The conference stage on our corporate page, a hotel ballroom with the house lights up and the windows uncovered, is that screen doing its job.
An ultra short throw projector at the base of an ambient light rejecting screen, holding a bright slide in an aircraft hangar with the door open to daylight.
Package two
## Long throw projector rental for ballrooms and larger rooms
When the room can go dark and the projector can live behind the audience or on a truss, a long throw setup gives you more placement freedom and a bigger image for the same money.
Rig Epson Pro EX10000 · 124 or 144 inch screen · long throw
The Epson Pro EX10000 is a 4,600 lumen Full HD laser projector with wireless and Miracast input, paired with either a 124 inch tab tensioned tripod screen or a 144 inch white matte screen depending on how far back the room lets us sit. Laser means full brightness the second it is switched on, and the same brightness at the end of a long conference day as at the start of it.
This is the workhorse for hotel ballrooms, banquet rooms, general session rooms, worship spaces and any room with real seating depth. Give us the ceiling height, the throw distance and the seating layout and we will tell you which of the two screens fits, then bring the one that does. Larger rooms sometimes want two screens so both sides of the audience read the slide straight on, and we rent projectors and screens in pairs for that reason.
Sizing
## What size projector screen do you need?
Audience size sets the screen, and the depth of the room sets it again. The rough guide below is where most Dallas-Fort Worth events land, and we will check it against your floor plan before anything is loaded on the truck.
### About 50 guests6 to 8 foot screen
Rig 1 projector · 6 to 8 ft screen · single feed
Boardrooms, training rooms, small breakouts and rehearsal dinners. At this size the back row is close enough that a modest screen still reads, and the projector matters more than the screen does. If the room has windows we will bring the ultra short throw setup instead, because a 6 foot image in a bright room is the easiest image on this page to lose.
### About 100 guests8 to 10 foot screen
Rig 1 projector · 8 to 10 ft screen · laptop and audio feed
Corporate meetings, association luncheons and mid size receptions. This is the projector and screen rental we deliver most often in Dallas. One screen at the front of the room, the projector paired to it for the throw distance we have, and a clean laptop connection at the podium so your presenter stands up and talks.
### About 150 guests10 to 12 foot screen
Rig 1 projector · 10 to 12 ft screen · dressed and skirted
Ballroom meetings, galas and fundraisers. At this size the screen becomes part of the room's look, so it gets dressed rather than left as a bare frame on legs. Rooms this deep also start to need a brighter projector, because the same lumens spread across a bigger image is a dimmer image.
### 200 guests and up12 to 16 foot screen
Rig 1 or 2 projectors · 12 to 16 ft screen · up to 150 in
General sessions, conferences, worship services and large weddings. Wide rooms usually do better with two screens than one very large screen, so the guests on the outside seats are looking straight at an image rather than across one. We rent screens up to 150 inches and will tell you honestly when your room wants a second projector and screen instead of a bigger single one.
Brightness
## How many lumens does your room need?
Lumens is the number people ask about, but the honest answer is that lumens and screen surface are one decision, not two.
### Room you can dim
3,000 to 4,000 lumens is enough for a ballroom or meeting room where the house lights come down and the shades close. Both of our projectors clear that comfortably, so in a dimmed room the screen size drives the choice rather than the brightness.
### Windows or lights on
A room with daylight or full house lights wants 5,000 lumens and up, or a projector paired with an ambient light rejecting screen, which is the route we take. The CLR screen buys back more contrast than the extra lumens would, and it does it with a projector that sits at the base of the screen.
### Screen surface does half the work
Two setups can put the same lumens on the wall and look completely different. Matte white spreads light evenly for wide seating, and the Light-On CLR surface rejects overhead light so the image survives with the lights up. We pick the surface for the room, then pick the projector that is paired to it.
### We check it in your room
Brightness on paper is a starting point. On the day we set the image, check it from the back row and the outside seats, and adjust before your first presenter walks up. If your room turns out brighter than the floor plan suggested, that is our problem to solve at setup, not yours.
